articles.title: ‘Our future is being stolen’: Greta Thunberg joins students protesting in Paris
articles.summary:
Swedish activist stands alongside French teenagers calling for investment to fix teacher shortages and crumbling schools

The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined demonstrating…

blocks.text: The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined demonstrating high school students in France as the country braced for another day of nationwide protests over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings.

“Young people are not being included in the conversation,” Thunberg, 23, who became famous as a teenager through school strikes demanding action on the climate crisis, told reporters outside the Lycée Paul Éluard in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.

As lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect pupils after multiple accusations of police brutality, she added: “Our future is being stolen from us and, as we have seen here, schools are not getting the investment they need.”

Now in their third week, the protests – backed by unionists, some teachers and radical leftwing opposition politicians – have shaken a government caught between calls for urgent public investment and pressure to reduce France’s ballooning deficit and debt.

Marches around the country drew more than 260,000 protesters last Tuesday and a further 75,000 on Thursday, according to interior ministry figures, and are expected to be repeated on Tuesday in several major cities including the French capital.

“They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them,” the university students’ union UE, many of whose members are also demonstrating in solidarity, posted on social media. High schools in Paris, Marseille and elsewhere were again blockaded.

French authorities had been hoping that the protests, some of which have resulted in violent clashes with French riot police, would ease up and eventually fizzle out during the two-week half-term school holidays due to start this weekend.

The education minister, Édouard Geffray, who has said 3,000 substitute teachers are being deployed in schools facing the most severe staff shortages, said on Tuesday he expected about 200 of the country’s 3,700 high schools to be completely closed.

French media have reported, however, that at least some classes have been cancelled or disrupted in many more schools, and some lycées – for pupils mostly aged between 15 and 18 – have switched wholly or partly to online learning.
after newsletter promotion

President Emmanuel Macron on Monday called for restraint, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”, as government figures showed more than 6,800 people – mainly minors – had been detained during the protests.

About 1,500 people are being prosecuted, the justice ministry has said, while 24 allegations of police brutality against demonstrators are under investigation. More than 200 teenagers, 100 school staff and 700 police officers have been injured.

One young protester has lost a hand from a police stun grenade, prompting the government to ban their use during the protests, while another lost the use of an eye and a third many of his teeth from a teargas canister fired at close range.

Rights groups and students have accused the police of a disproportionate use of force. Six months from a crucial presidential election to replace Macron, rival politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests.

The far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, has highlighted the damage to schools and called for parents ⁠to foot repair bills, while her radical-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.

articles.title: How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power
articles.summary: The judge who helped convict Jair Bolsonaro is caught up in a crisis that could benefit his son and damage Lula
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all.
“Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk.

Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup.

blocks.caption: Jair Bolsonaro supporters protest against Alexandre de Moraes in São Paulo in September 2024, a month after the supreme court justice ordered X to be suspended in Brazil. Photograph: Jorge Silva/Reuters

blocks.text: Now, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.

The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic.
Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal.

The crisis peaked last month with a ferocious exchange of insults between Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side – overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks.

Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back … the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis. His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula] paid the price for that institutional damage”.

Although analysts point to a range of reasons for the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election.

blocks.caption: Lula greets supporters at a campaign rally in Ceilândia this month. The president told the crowd he would win the election and that Brazil would not return to fascism. Photograph: André Borges/EPA

blocks.text: “These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right and has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters.

“We asked people about the court crisis, and they would say: ‘Everything is very confusing, but one thing we do know is that the big villain is Alexandre de Moraes,’” she said. “Precisely the judge who jailed Jair Bolsonaro now emerges, for these people, as the big corrupt figure and the main villain.”

Conrado Hübner Mendes, a professor of constitutional law at the University of São Paulo and a leading scholar of the supreme court, said Moraes put himself in that position by “embracing the role of heroic protagonist”.

The judge blocked some of Jair Bolsonaro’s moves during his government and drew the ire of far-right figures such as Musk and Donald Trump. The US went as far as to impose sanctions on him, in a move widely seen as an attempt to interfere in Jair’s trial.

On Monday, Moraes authorised Flávio Bolsonaro to resume visiting his father after a 90-day ban imposed in July, when the senator read out a letter from his father about the elections that Moraes considered a breach of Jair Bolsonaro’s ban on using social media.

Beyond the anger of Bolsonaro’s supporters, legal scholars and some on the Brazilian left, while acknowledging Moraes’s decisive role in the coup trial, also criticised several of his other rulings as authoritarian.
“He took on a huge responsibility, and now he has thrown that away in the most mediocre way possible, with this alleged corruption case,” said Mendes.

While acknowledging the contract between the law firm run by his wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and the disgraced banker – who is worth an extraordinarily large sum by Brazilian law firm standards – Moraes denied any wrongdoing. He said he had never ruled on any case involving Vorcaro and that there was therefore no conflict of interest.

Vorcaro has been behind bars since he was arrested in November as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. He is accused of leading a scheme through his Banco Master involving aggressive fundraising, unrealistic returns and falsified balance sheets that left an estimated £9bn hole, much of it involving public money and pensioners’ savings.

Text messages extracted from Vorcaro’s phone show that, two days before his arrest, the banker asked someone whom police later identified as Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes denies being the recipient and accuses a fellow justice, André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, of using the police against him for electoral reasons, allegedly to benefit Flávio’s campaign.

blocks.caption: Alexandre de Moraes has previously been likened by Elon Musk to the Harry Potter villain Lord Voldemort. Photograph: Carla Carniel/Reuters

blocks.text: Mendonça is one of the four other justices suspected of having links to Vorcaro. An institute he created is said to have taken out an £800,000 loan from one of the banker’s associates, though he says it has already been repaid. In the other justices’ cases, investigators uncovered links ranging from a £64m contract to an alleged stake in a fund that received £5.2m from Vorcaro. All deny wrongdoing.

No reports had linked Lula to the scandal until Friday, when Veja magazine reported that Vorcaro allegedly said he had paid £4.5m to finance a 2024 Oliver Stone documentary about the president. The federal police and the public prosecutor’s office, however, said the banker had neither made the allegation nor provided evidence to support it in his testimony. Lula denied receiving money from the banker.

Flávio Bolsonaro is being investigated over what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking Vorcaro to provide for a biopic about his father. One suspicion is that the money helped cover living and travel expenses for his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, during his self-imposed exile in the US, where he lobbied the Trump administration against Lula. The senator said all the money went towards sponsoring the film, which still has no release date.

blocks.caption: A girl plays with political flyers at the Cidade de Deus favela, in south-west Rio de Janeiro, on polling day. Photograph: Tercio Teixeira/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Besides Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead, the far right’s sweeping victory ensured an even more conservative congress in 2027, including the senate majority needed to impeach supreme court justices – a demand among his father’s supporters since the former president was convicted.

“With the scandal, the justices handed Bolsonarismo something it still didn’t have: an impeachable offence that could justify their removal,” said Mendes. “A court that ignores conflicts of interest and immerses itself in relationships with political and economic power is a court that has already become corrupted.”

Even if no justice is impeached, should Bolsonaro win, he could be entitled to fill four seats as justices retire during his term, leaving the court with at least six of its 11 members appointed by either him or his father.
“We can expect a court completely servile to the government,” Mendes said, adding that the separation of powers would be at risk and that the justices themselves bear part of the responsibility.
“The court ended up doing to itself the work an autocratic project needs – and brought itself down”.

articles.title: Millions of Medicaid recipients to face draconian requirements as of 1 January
articles.summary:
Trump’s reform law that seeks to make coverage harder to get, and to keep, includes working 80 hours per month

It is a date keeping US healthcare providers up at night: 1 January…

blocks.text: It is a date keeping US healthcare providers up at night: 1 January 2027.

As the midterm elections loom, everyone from hospital leaders and to patient advocates are focused on the New Year, when Republicans scheduled the most controversial elements of their healthcare reform law to go into effect.
Millions of Medicaid beneficiaries will be required, though a maze of government paperwork, to show they’re working 80 hours per month. And that’s just the marquee change.
“The costs to the family – and society as a whole – cannot be overstated,” said the American Academy of Pediatrics president, Dr Andrew Racine.

HR 1, also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” and signed into law by Donald Trump on 4 July 2025, cut roughly $1tn in federal spending from the healthcare industry – the biggest clawback of federal health spending ever. Paired with Republicans’ refusal to extend subsidies for plans in Obamacare marketplaces, the cuts are expected to result in about 17 million newly uninsured individuals through 2034.

Although the US has one of the most widely privatized healthcare systems in the world, nearly half of all health spending is paid for by government – whether federal, state or local, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid (CMS). Nearly 40% of US health spending in 2024 was from just two programs: Medicare and Medicaid, the public health insurance programs for the aging and low-income. To put the scale of the $1tn cut into context, Medicaid spent $937bn in 2024, according to the CMS.
As a result, advocates, researchers, hospital leaders and doctors are all expecting more medical debt, more delayed care and more people losing coverage for which they technically qualify.

“There couldn’t be a clearer link,” said Dr Luke Messac, an emergency physician at Mass General Brigham and a historian who has written about medical debt. “We saw that when Medicaid eligibility was expanded the flow of medical debt rapidly declined and sustained that decline.
“The easiest way to reverse that trend – to make medical debt more of a problem – is to yank people off Medicaid and leave them uninsured and unprotected.”

To understand Republicans’ new work requirements, you have to go all the way back to the Affordable Care Act (ACA) of 2010, when the Obama administration required states to expand Medicaid to cover people earning up to 138% of the federal poverty level, or about $16,000 for a single person today. Republicans hated this, and for the better part of a decade resisted the change through a supreme court case and dozens of Obamacare repeal votes.

However, over fits and starts, 44 states opted in. The deal was too sweet to pass up: states could insure many of their poorest residents and help their hospitals survive, with the overwhelming majority of the cost paid by the federal government.

Today, more than 82 million people rely on Medicaid for health insurance, or about 23% of the entire American public, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF), a health policy research organization. HR 1 is a direct assault on that system.

Consider first: the effects on regular people. Work requirements that go into effect in January will apply only to people in the 44 states that “expanded” Medicaid, and then only to people in the “expansion population”. That’s about 20 million people, according to KFF. Those people will need to prove they are working, going to school or volunteering at least 80 hours or earning $580 per month. People will also need to re-certify eligibility every six months, instead of every year. In short, Medicaid will be harder to get and harder to keep.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators hold signs during a press conference to discuss cuts to Medicaid on Capitol Hill in Washington DC on 13 May 2025.  Photograph: Nathan Howard/Reuters

blocks.text: KFF has come up with some hypothetical scenarios to illustrate how even qualified people might be tripped up by these bureaucratic hurdles. Consider Jane, who has a depressive disorder that does not qualify for an exemption from work requirements. In May, she experiences a depressive episode that makes it impossible for her to work 80 hours. In June, when her work requirement verification is due, her hours mean she is no longer eligible for Medicaid, and she becomes uninsured. Without insurance, she can no longer get her medication, which results in another depressive episode.

Or, consider John, who loses his job and is out of work in April and May. He gets a job in June, but his state requires people to satisfy three months of work before they are eligible for Medicaid. John does not satisfy this requirement, and is denied Medicaid. September 2026 will be the first month in a “look-back period” in some states.

“The insistence on these Medicaid work requirements, which is really just a way to decrease the rolls – that was the intention – is really going to increase the number of people with medical debt and the amount of medical debt in the system, which is bad not just for patients but for providers,” said Messac.
after newsletter promotion

HR 1 has wrought other changes too. Come January, Medicaid coverage will be winnowed down from three months of retroactive coverage to two months – or one depending on the applicant and the state. Alongside those changes in January are others that already went into effect. For instance, HR 1 made some legal immigrants ineligible for Medicaid. In the future, HR 1 will cut some accounting mechanisms that benefit children’s hospitals.

All of the different types of patients HR 1 will affect has created a long list of advocacy groups worried about the effects. Advocates for the elderly are worried some people won’t be able to get as much retroactive Medicaid coverage for nursing care, since the legislation shortened retroactive Medicaid benefits. (Elderly or unwell people often don’t file for Medicaid coverage for nursing care right away, either because they are too sick or falsely believe Medicare covers it.)

Advocates for children are worried parents will lose health insurance and have “spillover” to children. “When parents lose their health insurance, children may lose their coverage, too, even if they remain eligible,” said Racine.

Beyond the impacts on individuals: consider the systemic. One of the most common places to seek healthcare in the US is the hospital, for everything from births to cancer screenings. The Urban Institute estimates that HR 1 will cause $278bn in “uncompensated care” by 2034 – health industry parlance for unpaid bills. That puts hospitals in a bind, many of which operate on the thinnest imaginable margins.

“There is a consensus that, particularly in rural healthcare, there is this deepening crisis,” said Dr John Osborne, a former doctor at the Veterans Affairs administration in Washington state, and one of the organizers of a grassroots declaration of a rural health crisis in October. “I would say what’s happening in rural America is a harbinger of things to come throughout healthcare in the US.”

Although rural hospitals were a particular concern during passage – a closure can leave patients traveling hours for even routine care – new research shows both rural and urban hospitals are now closing at the same rate.

“Loss of access for acute care in-patient hospitals is not just a rural problem – it’s a national problem,” said Dr Thomas Tsai, a health policy researcher and surgeon at Brigham and Women’s hospital in Massachusetts and an author of the research.

That raises the possibility that even in urban cores, healthcare is inaccessible as patients from near and far crowd in to try to access care, including many newly uninsured people who will tend to use the emergency room more often.

“The impact will be profound,” said Dr John McCarthy, assistant dean for rural programs at the University of Washington School of Medicine, about HR 1. “Unless you have something that’s obviously really impressive, you have a five-hour wait – if you’re lucky.”

articles.title: [Kasalikasan] A visit to the homes at Smokey Mountain
articles.summary: 'At Smokey Mountain, despite its past and ongoing threat of relocation, people have made farms and communities'

blocks.text: I first heard of the issue at Smokey Mountain in 2024, when some Tondo residents trooped outside Manila City Hall. It was a protest against relocation and a proposed waste-to-energy facility.
Before that, I only knew of Smokey Mountain because of the pop group’s hit Paraiso and from a cursory knowledge of a violent demolition at the mountain of trash years ago.
Last May, I started arranging for a visit.

On a Thursday in early July, we hiked what is left of Smokey Mountain for a few minutes, and at the top, saw shelters, families, and dogs. There were trees and patches of land where people farm. The smell of garbage permeated the air. From the top, I saw the roofs of the housing tenements.

I talked to the residents on top of the mountain — one of them was a young girl named Jenny. She struck me because her voice was clear and she offered to read me a poem she wrote. It mattered that I saw her home and heard of her dreams.

A few days later, I attended a consultation for the Smokey Mountain rehabilitation and talked with an elderly woman seated next to me. She lives in one of the tenements and was among those dispersed in 1995. She had a story to tell. So we went back to Tondo to talk to her again, this time recorded on camera.
Then I wondered if the relocation site in Cavite would be convincing enough for informal settlers to uproot themselves. We visited the site to see the housing units for ourselves.

In late July, we spoke with Phil Ecology Systems Corporation. In August, we then spoke with the court-receiver managing the assets related to the Smokey Mountain development. I understood that the company is set on making profits, as is its nature, and the government has yet to settle obligations under this partnership to develop the area.

I began to see my visits to Smokey Mountain as a continuation of an exploration of the theme of home. Before I went to Tondo, my last fieldwork was in South Upi in Maguindanao del Sur, and in Marawi City. There are indigenous peoples struggling to protect their ancestral land in the Bangsamoro. There are people in Marawi City still calling for a safe and dignified return to their homes nine years after the siege.
And at Smokey Mountain, despite its past and ongoing threat of relocation, people have made farms and communities. What makes struggling for a disputed environment worthwhile is a home.
This documentary, which took months of fieldwork, reporting, writing, and editing, can be watched here. You can support our independent journalism by being a Rappler+ member.

articles.title: Travel nurses filling gaps in rural hospitals say they haven’t been paid for months
articles.summary: Emergency rooms in rural Saskatchewan often rely on travel nurses to stay open, but a group of those nurses say they've gone months without pay and the private agency that deployed them has gone…

image.caption: Esther Nagaga, left, and Shalu, who uses only one name, were hired through a private staffing agency called EZ Care. They say they are owed thousands of dollars. (Aishwarya Dudha)

blocks.text: A group of travel nurses say they haven't been paid in months and that the agency that employs them has gone "radio silent."
"We just would like to get paid for work," said Shalu, a travel nurse, said in an interview with CBC.

Shalu, who uses only one name, is an emergency room nurse currently contracted to work at the Parkland Integrated Health Centre in Shellbrook, Sask. As a travel nurse, she takes temporary contracts through agencies to fill staffing shortages at health-care facilities across Canada.

She said she started with EZCare, an Ontario-based staffing agency, on April 18 for a three-month contract, which she later renewed until the end of October. She had previously worked through the agency in 2024 without problems, except occasional pay delays, she said.
Shalu said she and around 20 other nurses hired through EZ Care across Canada received a letter from the agency around the end of July, warning of pay delays because of an "agency transition."
Nothing followed that letter, she said. A new company named in the letter never took over and the agency stopped paying her and around 25 other nurses, she said.

She said she's owed about $50,000 for around seven weeks of work and living expenses, from June 14 to Aug. 4, that would have been covered by the contract. CBC News reviewed bank statements that show she has not been paid.
Shalu and Nagaga say EZ Care, which is based out of Ontario, has not paid them for months. (EZ Care website)
"It is depressing some days. It hits me that I've worked for two months, and for nothing," she said.
CBC tried to reach EZ Care by phone and email but has not heard back.
'It is not fair': travel nurse
SHA spent $75.8 million on travel nurses in 2024-2025, according to Saskatchewan's provincial auditor's report this year.
Shalu says she is paid $86/hour, with time and a half for overtime, along with $40 per diem and $75/day for travel expenses.
"I'm feeling frustrated. There's nurses with families, cars and rent and accommodation to pay for," she said.
The group of unpaid nurses has been trying to contact the company, its owner, labour lawyers and the provincial government, but have had no success, Shalu said.
"It seems like all the doors are closed," she said.

The nurses stopped working temporarily after they realized they weren't getting paid. Shalu said that created staffing issues for the hospital and more burnout for nurses who were working without a fully staffed ER.

In a statement, the Saskatchewan Health Authority said it is aware of "payroll issues" between EZ Care and some of its nurses, but "cannot comment nor intervene in any contractual obligations between another employer and its contractors."

items: Regina is critically short of nuclear medicine technologists, say CUPE, NDP

blocks.text: "Patient care has not been impacted," SHA said.
The health authority said it hired EZ Care through an open request-for-proposals process, and that it is no longer requesting new contracts through the agency.

Esther Nagaga, another travel nurse working at the same hospital in Shellbrook, said she's missing two weeks of pay, worth around $20,000. Nagaga said she is paid $85/hour plus time and a half for overtime, along with a $40 per diem and $75/day for travel expenses.
"It's a long 12-hour shift with lots of hard work. Sometimes you're doing it alone. You're doing a lot of the work alone. So not getting compensated for it is very, it is not fair," Nagaga said.

items: Hospitals turn to staff for ideas to improve health care using AI

blocks.text: She reached out to the agency and got "radio silence," she said.

"I didn't know how I'm going to pay my next month's bills because it's Canada. We live paycheque to paycheque," she said. "We're doing the jobs we do because we need that extra money and we're taking time away from families."

Nagaga said hospital services and care delivered to patients were adversely affected because she and two other nurses, including Shalu, had stopped working at the facility after they found out they wouldn't be paid.
"The facility would have been impacted greatly because most of the time it was contract nurses that were working at that time," she said. "So that left the unit very short-staffed."
Independent contractors
Shalu said travel nurses are typically hired as independent contractors, not employees. She said labour lawyers they contacted told them that limits their options.

David Camfield, a professor of labour studies and sociology at the University of Manitoba, said the nurses' situation raises questions about whether they should have been classified as "contractors" and the deeper issues with the health system's reliance on agencies.

"There's a big difference between someone who's a genuinely independent contractor … and someone who's been classified as an independent contractor, but whose actual relationship to the employer is really one of an employee," he said in an interview.
LISTEN | What will it take to retain nurses in the province?:
Blue Sky50:02What will it take to retain nurses in the province?

Camfield described SHA's travel nurse situation as a "triangular relationship." On paper, the agency is the employer paying the nurses. Day to day, though, the nurses are managed by Saskatchewan Health Authority staff, which makes the SHA the de facto employer, he said.

He said the bigger problem is the public health-care system's reliance on agencies to fill vacancies. That leaves facilities without stable, permanent staff, which he said is bad for everyone who uses public health care.
"We really need to be asking questions about why is the health-care system being starved of the necessary resources that would be needed to provide nurses with stable, high-quality jobs," he said.
"I think it would be a mistake to let either of them off the hook here."
The nurses said they asked the SHA to withhold payment to EZ Care and pay them directly, but that SHA refused because its contract was with the agency, not the nurses.
Shalu and Nagaga are back at work now, working through a different agency. They hoping the SHA can still help them get paid for the work they did.

articles.title: Impeachment court lifts sub judice rule on withdrawn charges vs Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Rule 18 bars involved parties from publicly discussing the merits of an ongoing impeachment trial

blocks.text: PRESIDING OFFICER. Impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero addresses the court on August 25, 2026.
Voltaire Domingo/Senate Social Media Unit
Rule 18 bars involved parties from publicly discussing the merits of an ongoing impeachment trial

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday, October 13, lifted the sub judice rule on three withdrawn impeachment articles against Vice President Sara Duterte, allowing the parties to publicly discuss the dropped charges.
The decision drew objections from lead defense counsel Sheila Sison, who warned that abandoning Rule 18 midway through the trial could undermine the integrity of the proceedings.

The three withdrawn articles cover the alleged misuse of confidential funds (Article I), bribery (Article III), and grave threats (Article IV). The court earlier granted the House prosecution panel’s request to withdraw these charges, leaving only Article II, which involves Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

“We actually object to the abandonment of Rule 18 if we are to be true and faithful to the rationale and wisdom of the sub judice rule that not only permeates this court, it permeates the entire judicial system,” Sison said.

“It is needed to maintain the integrity of the proceedings. There should not be any single instance or occasion that this should be abandoned in the middle of trial and right before the defense or respondent presents her case,” she added.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero explained that relaxing Rule 18 was intended to allow Duterte to respond to the withdrawn articles both inside and outside the courtroom.

“The reason behind the relaxing of Rule 18 was more to afford, actually, the respondent to respond in the manner she may deem fit both in this courtroom, subject to the objections and ruling of the court, and outside,” Escudero said.

Amid the defense’s objections, Senator-judge Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan moved to reconsider the ruling and maintain the enforcement of Rule 18 pending a possible motion for reconsideration from the defense.
“If the court agrees, pending a possible motion for reconsideration when we resume, then Rule 18 should continue to be enforced and not abandoned,” Pangilinan said.
Pangilinan also moved to authorize Escudero to issue a resolution on the matter during the trial break. Senator-judge Joel Villanueva seconded the motion.
Defense lawyer Michael Poa cited a gag order issued by a Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) in connection with the separate grave threats case against Duterte.
“We just wanted the court to know that the difficulty we’re facing with this, well, lifting of Rule 18 as regards to those articles,” Poa said.
“For example, for grave threat, we have a gag order from the RTC, Your Honor, trying that case on speaking on it. So in a way, the prosecution can discuss it but we cannot,” he added.

Escudero said his earlier ruling would remain in effect unless the defense indicated otherwise. He added that Pangilinan’s motion for reconsideration would be taken up, with the court deciding whether to reconsider the ruling in whole or in part.

“After which, the motion for reconsideration of Senator-judge Francis Pangilinan will come into operation as it will be recorded by the clerk and the reconsideration of that rule shall be made either in whole or in part,” Escudero said.

Rule 18 of the Senate impeachment rules bars the presiding officer, senator-judges, prosecutors, the respondent, their counsel, and witnesses from publicly commenting on or disclosing the merits of an ongoing impeachment trial, including through online platforms.
In August, Escudero ordered the strict enforcement of the sub judice rule. – Rappler.com

articles.title: AFP backs Gibo Teodoro amid Chinese Embassy's criticism of severed military dialogue
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday rallied behind Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. after a Chinese Embassy rant on the severed military dialogue…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 5:46pm

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday rallied behind Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro Jr. after a Chinese Embassy rant on the severed military dialogue between Manila and Beijing.

“The DND’s decision to suspend military-to-military communication channels with PRC, three (3) years ago, was based on experience and the consistent failure of these mechanisms to produce meaningful results amid continued provocative and irresponsible actions by their People’s Liberation Army and China Coast Guard,” the AFP said in a statement.

“Upholding the Constitution and safeguarding our sovereign rights is a duty incumbent upon every Filipino. United as one nation, the Filipino people and the AFP will continue to defend our territorial integrity,” the organization added.
In a statement on Monday, October 12, the Chinese Embassy accused Teodoro of suspending the military-to-military communication between China and Philippines for his “political self interests.”
“Everyone knows that no matter how difficult bilateral relations become, communication channels should remain open to avoid miscalculation and prevent tensions from escalating,” the embassy said.

“But Gibo Teodoro decided to shut down mil-mil communication between China and the Philippines for political self interests. His move fuels mistrust, narrows the space for crisis management, and pushes frontline personnel closer to confrontation,” it added.
In response, Teodoro noted that the said dialogue channel between Manila and Beijing was already suspended a long time ago.

“Here we go again… Military-to-military ties have long been suspended—for roughly three years now. They said this again because it's a desperate move on their part—because they were caught in their own 'foolishness’,” he said in Filipino in a Facebook post.

The Defense Dept. also reposted on Facebook the statement released in May 2024, noting the discontinuation of the communications between the department and the Chinese Embassy after Teodoro assumed office in July 2023. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Escudero: Senator-judges may seek reconsideration of ruling on dropped articles
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero said Tuesday that senator-judges may still seek reconsideration of the court's ruling allowing the House prosecution panel to withdraw…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published October 13, 2026 5:41pm

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero said Tuesday that senator-judges may still seek reconsideration of the court's ruling allowing the House prosecution panel to withdraw three of the four articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte.

Escudero made the clarification after Senator-Judge Bam Aquino asked whether the decision to withdraw Articles I, III and IV, which detail allegations of misuse of confidential funds, bribery and grave threats, respectively, was made by the impeachment court or the prosecution.
“Hiniling ng prosekusyon, pinagpasiyahan ng korte (The prosecution manifested this, and the court acted on it),” Escudero said in response.
Escudero clarified that the ruling could still be challenged through an appeal or a motion for reconsideration once the parties have had time to consult their clients or reflect on the matter.

“It is a ruling of the Chair that, like any other ruling, is subject to either appeal or reconsideration at the proper time once they have had enough time to, as you said, either consult their clients or reflect on the matter," he said.
"Of course, fully understanding that the appeal or reconsideration would have to be made by a senator-judge on the matter,” Escudero added.
Aquino then asked whether the defense team could still seek reconsideration of the court's decision after consulting Duterte.
“A senator-judge can [move for reconsideration],” Escudero answered.
The presiding officer, however, said he believed the defense was not objecting to the prosecution's motion to withdraw the three articles.
Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison confirmed this, saying the prosecution's decision should not preempt the respondent's decision on how to address the allegations against her.

“This decision to withdraw those articles is the prosecution’s lookout. And so, whatever consequences of those withdrawals, they should be able to bear alone without the respondent suffering any consequences from that decision,” Sison said.

She said the defense would consult Duterte but stressed that the prosecution’s decision to withdraw the three impeachment articles should not dictate how the Vice President or her legal team would present their evidence.

“However, we really need to record the fact that our objection on whatever idea that may be floating at this moment, that this decision of the prosecution will somehow make decisions for how the respondent or the defense will present our evidence in chief,” she added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: UK holiday demand may have peaked amid cost of living squeeze, says travel industry
articles.summary: Spain remains most popular destination as Britons book later in hope of better deals, Abta report finds

blocks.text: The UK’s cost of living squeeze means fewer people plan to ringfence money for holiday abroad next year, the travel industry warned on Tuesday.

Despite war, wildfires and EES border checks, the numbers of Britons taking holidays climbed back to pre-pandemic levels this year – but rising costs may mean the numbers have peaked, according to an annual travel industry report.
Numbers taking holidays both at home and abroad continued to rise, although late bookings and shorter city breaks have been an increasing feature of holidays through 2026.

Confidence in travel dropped slightly year on year but rebounded as fears over jet fuel shortages and flight disruption faded since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran in February, according to research from the industry body Abta.
Overall, 88% of Brits took a holiday this year, matching the 2019 pre-pandemic peak, with a new high of 74% in the UK and 62% abroad.

However, Abta’s report found that almost one in three people were planning to spend less on travelling abroad next year, suggesting that the annual holiday is no longer sacrosanct. Fewer people now say they are willing to reduce spending on phones or other gadgets than the holiday abroad.

Abta said the holiday business remained resilient, despite a dip in its travel confidence index to +50 – this measures the net proportion of people who felt secure in going abroad, compared with those who were worried. But it said that score had rebounded since disruption from the Middle East conflict and fears about fuel availability and the EU’s entry/exit system (EES).

The Abta chief executive, Mark Tanzer, said it “had been a tough year for the travel industry”. But he added: “Demand has held up well despite a range of challenges this year, and that looks set to continue, as does the willingness to prioritise spending on travel over other discretionary items.”
Speaking at the annual Abta travel convention in Madeira, Tanzer added: “It’s been a stop-start year but the market did come back in the summer.
“We saw people switching their holiday plans and booking later, waiting and seeing – maybe hoping for better deals but also managing the uncertainty.”

He said the industry would continue to lobby ministers hard to reduce aviation taxes and increase help in the switch to sustainable aviation fuels, to help cut costs and support an industry that contributed £57bn to the UK economy.
after newsletter promotion
Tanzer said the investment in tourism continued but he admitted: “The pressures of the last few months are not going to go away in the next 18 months.”
Spain increased its dominance of the British outbound market. The number who said they visited Spain was up four percentage points to 36%, while Portugal moved up to sixth in popularity for holidays.

Polling next year’s travel intentions, only 26% said they were planning to visit Spain, with places such as Japan and Norway cited in the top 10. However, previous surveys have underlined that, despite dreams of somewhere more exotic, Britons head resolutely back to Spain.
Travel to the convention was provided by Abta

articles.title: Ex-Chicago detective identified as killing child in 65-year cold case
articles.summary:
Police used recently discovered DNA to pin murder of eight-year-old girl on Thomas McInerney, who died in 2006

Chicago police on…

blocks.text: Chicago police on Monday said they recently used newly discovered DNA evidence to tie the 1960 murder of an eight-year-old girl to one of its own former homicide detectives.

Thomas McInerney had been dead for 20 years by the time authorities issued a statement identifying him as the killer of Gloria Kowalewicz – well after retiring from the Chicago police department (CPD) and two federal public defender’s offices in Nevada where he worked as an investigator.
Nonetheless, the CPD’s statement expressed a hope that the news about McInerney “brings a measure of closure to all who knew Gloria and her story”.
“McInerney should have never worn the CPD star,” the statement added. “And it is devastating to accept that he was never identified and held accountable while he was alive.”

The Chicago Tribune was the first to report on the exposure of McInerney as Gloria’s murderer – recounting in a lengthy article on Sunday how the girl’s killing, which shocked the city, was solved more than six decades later by DNA evidence gathered from a genetic ancestry website.
Gloria was last seen alive on the morning of 12 November 1960 as she walked from her family’s West Englewood neighborhood home to a mass at a nearby church.

She never made it to the service. Someone abducted her on the way and fatally shot her, and within hours her body was found discarded in a ditch at a forest preserve south-west of Chicago, police said in their statement.

Police said they secured various pieces of evidence at the scene where Kowalewicz had apparently been murdered – including a bullet, her coat and a white communion purse with a prayer book inside. “Investigators also lifted a fingerprint from the strap of Gloria’s purse,” police noted.
Meanwhile, the Tribune reported that police – along with volunteers from the ranks of local firefighters, Boy Scouts and military veterans – mounted a large search for the girl’s killer.
A police-headed taskforce interviewed about 1,300 people in connection with Gloria’s slaying, among them a dozen individuals who were given lie-detector tests while being questioned.
Police said none of that allowed them to identify a suspect, however.
Yet that changed earlier in 2026 when DNA submitted to a family tree website enabled the FBI to join McInerney to the scene of Gloria’s murder, according to the Tribune.

Further DNA, fingerprint and ballistic testing then established that McInerney – a US army veteran who lived around the corner from the girl – had killed Gloria the CPD said in its statement on Monday.
McInerney joined the Chicago police force in 1959, said his obituary, which was published after his death on 30 August 2006. He was about to turn 25 at the time of Gloria’s murder.

The obituary said McInerney was investigating homicides for the CPD when he retired from the agency in 1987. He then worked as investigator for the federal public defender’s offices in Las Vegas and Reno, Nevada, until his retirement in 2004.

McInerney’s obituary also touted his receiving “numerous commendations during his years with the [CPD]” – as well as his being recognized as outstanding federal defender investigator in 2003. It described him as a husband, a father to two sons and three daughters, and a grandfather to a dozen children.

The CPD statement on Monday made it a point to say that Gloria’s parents died without ever knowing who had murdered their daughter. The agency called McInerney’s “abhorrent”, saying: “They not only took the life of an eight-year-old child – but left … all who knew and loved her shattered as they searched for answers.”

Gloria’s brother, Adam Kowalewicz, told the Tribune that it was a relief to learn his sister’s murderer had been identified. But he said to the outlet that he was frustrated McInerney had died at age 70 without ever being made to face justice.
“He never paid his dues,” Adam Kowalewicz said to the Tribune. “You hope he’s going to pay his dues with the good lord.”

articles.title: Palace: Marcos’ ‘buy buckets’ advice part of ‘serious’ El Niño preparations
articles.summary: Marcos urged the public to prepare buckets and containers as the government plans to roll out an information campaign on collecting, filtering and treating rainwaters for safe usage.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 5:27pm

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang defended President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s advice for the public to buy "balde" or buckets in preparation for anticipated water shortages due to El Niño, saying the remark was part of the government's "serious" readiness efforts.

At a press briefing on Tuesday, October 13, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro addressed the public criticism surrounding Marcos’ advice, saying it was not a joke and should be taken seriously as the impact of El Niño could worsen in the coming months.

“Sineseryoso ng pangulo ang magaganap at nagaganap na at maaaring mag-worsen sa mga susunod na buwan. Ang bawat pagtalakay dito, ang bawat mensahe, ang bawat suggestion, ang bawat mga binibigay na aral sa atin ng gobyerno at ng pangulo, ito ay dapat na sineseryoso,” Castro said.

(The president takes the potential impacts and the current effects [of El Niño] that could worsen in the coming months. Each discussion about it, each message, each suggestion, each lesson given by the government and the president should be taken seriously.)
On October 11, Marcos urged the public to prepare buckets and containers as the government plans to roll out an information campaign on collecting, filtering and treating rainwater for safe use.

“Bumili na kayo ng balde para kapag umulan, makolekta na ninyo lahat. Tuturuan namin kayo…we’ll give you the filter. We’ll teach you how to do everything para hindi kayo magkasakit at maayos ang pag-treat ng tubig,” Marcos said.

(Buy buckets so when it rains, you’ll collect the water. We will teach you…we’ll give you the filter. We’ll teach you how to do everything so you will not be sick and the treatment of water will be proper.)

Castro confirmed at Tuesday’s press briefing that the buckets are intended for rainwater collection methods that the government, particularly the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), intends to teach the public.
“Magsasagawa po mismo si Secretary Rex Gatchalian ng video patungkol dito para po kayo ay maturuan,” Castro said.
(Secretary Rex Gatchalian will make a video to teach you about this.)
Authorities have earlier warned that water shortages are highly likely during the El Niño season, urging the public to conserve water as early as now.
This October, the National Water Resources Board (NWRB) reduced the water allocation for Metro Manila residents from the regular 50 to 53 cubic meters per second to 44 cubic meters per second.
The Palace spokesperson also addressed the “obstructionists,” whom she said only noticed and amplified the negative aspects of the administration’s efforts.
“Kailangan po talaga natin ng balde-baldeng utak para po maintindihan niyo po kung ano ang plano ng pangulo,” Castro said.
(We really need buckets of brains so you’ll understand the plans of the president.)

articles.title: Impeachment court lifts sub judice rule on withdrawn raps vs. Sara Duterte
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court, in allowing the prosecution to drop three articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte, also lifted the sub judice rule on the withdrawn raps.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 5:22pm
The Senate impeachment court, in allowing the prosecution to drop three articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte, also lifted the sub judice rule on the withdrawn raps.

According to the ruling read by presiding officer Senator-Judge Francis Escudero, the lifting of Rule 18 is meant to allow the parties particularly the respondent Vice President to "address, explain, and respond to any matter contained in those withdrawn articles.”

The prosecution panel on Tuesday informed the court that it was withdrawing Article 1 on the alleged misuse of confidential funds, Article 3 on bribery, and Article 4 on assassination plot, grave threats, and inciting to sedition.
The impeachment court accepted the prosecution's manifestation and, among others, ruled that the defense panel may only present evidence on Article 2 or the case on alleged unexplained wealth.
The prosecution had already presented evidence on Article 1 and 4.

“Rule 18 requires the parties, their counsel, witnesses, and other persons covered by the rules to refrain from making public comments or disclosures concerning the merits of matters pending adjudication before the Impeachment Court," Escudero said.

"Upon the effectivity of this Order, the separate merits of Articles 1, 3 and 4 are no longer pending for adjudication. Accordingly, the prosecutors, the Respondent, their respective counsel, and witnesses may publicly address, explain, and respond to any matter contained in those withdrawn Articles,” he added.

“In particular, the Respondent, given that she will no longer have any opportunity or need to defend against those allegations through the presentation of evidence before this Court. She may therefore answer them, present her account, and defend her conduct and reputation in public discourse,” Escudero said.

The impeachment court presiding officer, however, said such freedom to discuss the allegations in the withdrawn Articles does not authorize the unrestricted disclosure or dissemination of the evidence presented in connection with them.

“Withdrawal does not declassify evidence, remove an existing seal or protective order, waive any privilege, or extinguish duties arising from privacy, statutory secrecy, witness protection, legal ethics, confidentiality undertakings, or the sensitive character of the material,” Escudero said.

“Evidence subject to any such protection shall not be copied, reproduced, photographed, circulated, published, uploaded, transmitted, or otherwise disseminated to the public, except as expressly permitted by law or by an order of this Court,” Escudero added.

Escudero, however, stressed that Rule 18 will still apply to the pending Article 2 which alleges accumulation of unexplained wealth over non-declaration of assets and non-divestment of business interests in violation of a Constitutional ban.

“This freedom extends only to Articles 1, 3 and 4 and does not authorize public comment or disclosure concerning the merits of the retained Article 2, which remains pending before the Cour," he said. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte physically appears in court at ICC fourth status conference
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte was physically present in court at the ICC on Tuesday morning (Tuesday afternoon, Philippines time) for the fourth status conference in his case.

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published October 13, 2026 5:21pm

Former president Rodrigo Duterte listens through headphones in court at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, The Netherlands on Tuesday, October 13, 2026 during the fourth status conference in his case. Screenshot from ICC livestream

Former president Rodrigo Duterte was physically present in Chamber III at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, The Netherlands on Tuesday morning (Tuesday afternoon, Philippines time) for the fourth status conference in his case.
The conference is set to discuss procedural matters in Duterte’s case. This marks his third appearance before the tribunal. His first appearance was via video conference.
His first physical appearance was during the third status conference in September.
The former president’s current appearance comes days after the ICC declared him physically and mentally well enough to stand trial.
Duterte was assessed by medical experts, saying that he showed no sign of worsening mental abilities.

The former Philippine president was arrested by Philippine authorities and turned over to the ICC in 2025. He faces charges of crimes against humanity in connection to the bloody war on drugs, which saw the deaths of at least 6,000 people. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Anne Aly reveals she has received 19 death threats in the last week alone
articles.summary:
After an MP said she should be ‘shamed and stoned’, federal minister hit back at ‘racist and misogynistic’ language

  • Get our

blocks.text: Anne Aly has condemned as “racist” and “misogynistic” comments in parliament calling for her to be “stoned in the square” – while revealing she has received 19 death threats in the last week alone.

Gold Coast Liberal National MP, Angie Bell, the member for Moncrieff, told the House of Representatives that Aly, the small business minister, and the prime minister should be “shamed and stoned in the square” over a decision made by the tax office.
Bell was forced to withdraw the comment by the speaker.
On Instagram, Aly responded with an emotive post-to-camera, saying she had been the subject of consistent death threats, including previous threats that she should be stoned.

“I don’t usually comment about these sorts of things, but I feel like I have to. This past week alone, I’ve had 19 death threats on my social media. And in the past I’ve had death threats that are couched in that exact same language: stone her.”
Aly said that the comments directed at her were not just unparliamentary, but fundamentally inimical to Australian values.
“We are a country that proudly stands against violence against women and against regimes that use brutal methods like stoning against women.
“This is not just something that we should just turn away from.
“It is racist. It is misogynistic. And it is something that should never have been said.”
Bell made the remarks before question time on Tuesday as part of an opposition attack on the government over the Australian Tax Office’s decision to ban credit card payments used to pay tax bills.
Bell said millions of Australians were employed by small businesses, and would be harmed by the decision.
“This minister and this prime minister should be absolutely shamed and stoned in the square,” she said.
Bell was forced by the speaker to withdraw the comments after the government’s leader of the house, Tony Burke, raised concerns with what he said was “physically violent imagery”.
Australia – like other liberal democracies – has experienced a dramatic rise in threats against politicians and other public figures.
after newsletter promotion

More than 50 police reports on a range of alleged criminal offences were made during the last federal election campaign and the Australian Federal Police received 951 referrals or threats against parliamentarians in the 2024-25 financial year, an increase of more than 60% in just four years.

Last year, AFP commissioner, Reece Kershaw, told Senate estimates that female politicians were particular targets, and that “the nature of threats and comments directed at female parliamentarians and high office holders is particularly troubling, with a common feature being offensive material centred on derogatory language about their appearance”.
“Some of this material also contains extremely violent themes, including threats of graphic, sexual violence,” he said.
“These threats, which are being made online or are being sent in the post or over the phone, are sometimes also directed at their children.”
Kershaw said politicians were targeted because of their public profiles, or because of their policy positions.
“However, in some cases, it appears male offenders are targeting women because they are women. The AFP will not tolerate this criminality and will take swift action.”

articles.title: US emergency call records reveal confusion after failed execution of Christa Pike
articles.summary: The killer of Colleen Slemmer was ultimately taken to hospital after two doses of lethal injection did not kill her.

blocks.text: Emergency call records have revealed the confusion that developed among prison staff and emergency call handlers after the execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike went wrong last month in Tennessee.

Pike, 50, who killed Colleen Slemmer alongside her then-boyfriend in 1995, was given two doses of lethal injection on 30 September. Once it became clear that she was not going to die from the dosage, she was taken to hospital.
The confusion resulted in part from an apparent disconnect between prison staff, according to the AP news agency, which first obtained audio of the emergency calls.
This allegedly delayed Pike's treatment. The BBC has asked the state corrections department for comment.

The department has not yet stated what it thinks went wrong in the attempted execution of Pike. Pike's legal team has offered the explanation that the pentobarbital chemical, with which she was injected, probably spread under skin rather than reaching her bloodstream in a sufficient quantity to kill her.

Pike has now been discharged from hospital, though in their most recent update on her health, her team cautioned that she faced a "long road to recovery". It is not clear what treatment, if any, she is receiving now that she is back in prison.
Her case is now in uncharted territory as she is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".
Pike's boyfriend at the time of the murder, Tadaryl Shipp, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty because he was not yet an adult when the crime was committed.

The sequence of events on the evening of 30 September was pieced together by US media using a combination of emergency call recordings and transcripts. The records were published in full by the Nashville Banner, external news outlet.

The initial call made from Riverbend Prison - which was reportedly made at 20:40 local time - was considered to have been false by first responders, after the caller was unable to verify themselves using a code.

That person seems to have been in a part of the prison where the injections were taking place. They said: "We've been carrying out an execution tonight. We've administered 10 grams of pentobarbital. The person is not yet deceased. That started approximately one hour ago. And we're calling for an ambulance."
The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications released records of its conversations with other local agencies as it tried to confirm whether the call was genuine.

The confusion appears to have been compounded by other prison staff, from the institution's central command, who said at 21:07 that they "would have been the ones to call in" and that they "did not make that call".

It was not until about 21:11 that prison officials verified that the initial call, made about half an hour previously, had in fact been genuine. At that point, the emergency responders were allowed through the prison gates.

A later call acknowledged that the situation had been chaotic. At 21:34, as Pike was being taken to hospital, one medic asked a colleague to ensure the prison knew where Pike was being taken, "just 'cause there's been so much other confusion".

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Quezon City disputes claims of DILG fire truck, ambulance turnover
articles.summary: The Quezon City government clarified that the turnover took place in Quezon province, based on a DILG press release

blocks.text: Claim: The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) turned over fire trucks and ambulances to Quezon City under the government’s “Bawat Buhay Mahalaga” campaign.
Why we fact-checked this: The claim was posted by the Facebook page Quezon City Updates on October 7. As of writing, it has accumulated over 315,000 reactions, 24,000 comments, and 21,000 shares.
The post shows photos of the vehicles allegedly set to be delivered to the city, meant to help provide faster government services.

“Layunin nitong palakasin ang kakayahan ng mga lokal na pamahalaan sa pagtugon sa sunog, aksidente at iba pang emergency, upang mas mabilis na marespondehan ang bawat insidente at mas maprotektahan ang buhay ng mga mamamayan,” the post reads.
(It aims to strengthen the local government’s capability to respond to fires, accidents, and other emergencies, enabling faster incident response and better protection of citizens’ lives.)
The facts: The Quezon City government clarified in a Facebook post on October 8 that no fire trucks or ambulances from the DILG were turned over to the city.
It also clarified that it has no affiliation with the page that posted the claim, advising the public to refer to its official social media accounts for verified information.

“Walang katotohanan ang kumakalat na post sa social media tungkol sa umano’y pamamahagi ng ‘fire truck’ at ‘ambulance’ sa Quezon City mula sa Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG). Base sa inilabas na press release ng DILG, ang turnover ay isinagawa sa ‘QUEZON PROVINCE’ at hindi sa Quezon City,” the post read.

(There is no truth to the post circulating on social media about the alleged distribution of ‘fire trucks’ and ‘ambulances’ in Quezon City from the Department of the Interior and Local Government. Based on the press release issued by the DILG, the turnover was conducted in ‘Quezon Province’ and not in Quezon City.)

On October 7, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla led the turnover of 30 Unified 911 emergency response motorcycles to the Quezon Police Provincial Office. During the event, Remulla also announced that the department is set to procure new fire trucks as part of a major push to modernize the Bureau of Fire Protection’s fleet.

Viral ‘fire trike’ claims: A similar claim circulated on social media around the same time alleging that the DILG bought fire trikes priced at P10 million each, to be distributed to different local government units.
Remulla clarified in an interview that the agency did not buy the small fire tricycles shown in the viral posts. He said the Nueva Ecija local government bought those vehicles back in July.

The interior secretary made the clarification as the photos of the small fire tricycles were linked to the DILG’s plan to buy 1,500 fire trucks next year. The planned purchase aims to address the country’s fire truck shortage and replace aging equipment. According to the DILG, the procurement is expected to save the government P9 billion, with each unit priced at P10 million, down from the previous P16 million price tag.
The agency added that its representatives went to Korea to establish a government-to-government agreement for the purchase. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Farage denies Reform would let troops shoot small boats after Jenrick’s ‘lethal force’ claim
articles.summary: Party leader says Jenrick’s comments ‘misconstrued’, after MP said Royal Marines would be allowed to fire at those on boats

blocks.text: Nigel Farage has denied that a Reform UK government would authorise lethal force against migrant crossings in the Channel, hours after one of his MPs said the Royal Marines should be permitted to fire on the boats.
Robert Jenrick, a Reform UK MP who defected from the Conservatives, had told TalkTV that the party would deploy the Royal Marines to take boats back to France.

“What we are going to do, and we’re the only political party that has the courage to say this, is deploy the Royal Marines into the Channel. If they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so,” he said.
But speaking on LBC, Farage said he would not authorise routine use of force, that it would be used only if soldiers were fired at, and that Jenrick was being “utterly misconstrued”.

“Anybody wearing British military uniform who gets fired at has the right to respond. That’s what he was saying,” he said. “Remember, in these camps, every week there are shootings, there are stabbings.
“We are dealing here with very, very serious international criminal organisations, and what we’re saying is, we will, if we win the next election, pick these people up and take them back to France.

“There is a possibility that initially that might be met with some force. If it is, force will be met with force. But I tell you something: within two weeks of boats being taken back to France, the boats will stop coming.”

Jenrick had said that allowing the use of force would mean the problem would end “in just a few days.” He said using force was “obviously not what we want to see happen”, adding: “We want to see these individuals picked up off the boats in a sensible and reasonable way, and taken straight back to France.”
The defence minister Luke Pollard called the comments “disgusting and illegal”, and said that the armed forces were not allowed to accept “an illegal order”.

“We do not shoot unarmed civilians. We do not take military action against civilians,” Pollard told Times Radio. “The idea of this is a soundbite designed by Reform to distract from their sleaze and their scandal … it’s abhorrent to military values, it’s abhorrent to British values.
“I don’t think anyone should give this any truck. We can all see what this is: an attempt to distract from Reform’s internal woes.”

articles.title: Child safety staff determined to send Elizabeth Struhs home with parents despite doctors’ concerns, inquest hears
articles.summary:
Queensland coronial inquest into death of eight-year-old girl continues after 14 members of religious sect were convicted of her manslaughter



It was impossible to change the mind…

blocks.text: It was impossible to change the mind of child safety staff after they had decided to send Elizabeth Struhs home with her parents despite some of her doctors’ concerns, a police officer has told a coronial inquest into the young girl’s death.

Child safety staff decided in 2019 that it would be “more detrimental” to not return Elizabeth, aged six at the time, to her Toowoomba home upon her discharge from hospital after suffering a coma due to diabetic ketoacidosis, a Queensland coroner heard.

Elizabeth died at home on 7 January 2022 after her parents withdrew the insulin she needed to survive type 1 diabetes. Her parents were members of a religious sect known as the Saints. The sect did not believe in medicine, and believed Elizabeth would be miraculously healed of her illness or raised from the dead, the inquest heard.
All 14 adult members of the sect were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including her father, Jason Struhs, and mother, Kerrie Struhs.

The coroner, Ainslie Kirkegaard, heard evidence on Monday from senior doctors at the Queensland children’s hospital who had repeatedly raised the alarm after Elizabeth was hospitalised in a 2019 incident.

Kerrie Struhs told the authorities at the time that she didn’t believe in medicine, and had discouraged Elizabeth’s father from seeking medical assistance and to instead trust in prayer, the coroner heard.
Both parents were convicted of not providing the necessaries of life to Elizabeth as a result of the incident, and Kerrie was jailed.

After Elizabeth was admitted to hospital in 2019, doctors warned that Kerrie might “sabotage” her long-term treatment for the incurable illness, which requires multiple insulin injections a day, if they lived together, the coroner heard.
But the court heard that child safety officers determined she should be returned home to the care of Jason.

The coroner heard evidence about a meeting held by the suspected child abuse and neglect team in which the decision was made. It was led by child safety officers, but involved specialist police and health staff.
Jason was deemed to be able to provide treatment for Elizabeth, such as insulin injections, the court heard.

According to minutes from the meeting, a child safety officer said: “The Queensland children’s hospital is not agreeing with our assessment and have been very vocal about it. I feel that removing her would be more detrimental and we currently have the father stepping up.”
On Tuesday, the court heard from a police officer who had attended the meeting. He told the court he’d served as a child safety liaison for 10 years.
“I learned early on … you couldn’t change child safety’s mind once they had made their decision,” the officer told the court.
“I was never going to change their mind regardless of what I said.”
The officer said the attitude was not confined to a single child safety officer.
after newsletter promotion
“It was across the board … they had their own structured decision making tools that they used and we had to respect their decision.”
The officer described the approach as “professional courtesy”.

Jason was initially willing to provide insulin to Elizabeth – against the wishes of his wife and their other children – but ceased doing so in 2021 after converting to his wife’s religious beliefs and joining her church group, leading to the child’s death.

A paediatrician specialist in child safety based at the Toowoomba hospital told the inquest on Tuesday that she was “generally happy” with the way child safety approached the case, including returning Elizabeth home.
According to notes taken at a meeting at the time and presented in court, the specialist said Elizabeth would be safe “as long as they are engaging with the hospital and diabetes educator”.
“If they stop showing up or engaging then it is likely we would put in a report as we would need to try and find out why.”
On Monday, two other doctors at the Queensland children’s hospital in Brisbane told the inquest that they were unhappy with the approach, which one labelled “entirely inadequate to address the risk”.

One told the coroner that there had been longstanding poor relations between the Brisbane and Toowoomba hospitals, and their advice was ignored. But the Toowoomba doctor denied the hospitals had a poor relationship.
No witnesses appearing at the inquest can be identified for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Ship sinks in new drone attack off Bulgaria, PM summons Russian ambassador
articles.summary: Bulgaria's prime minister says two merchant ships were hit by drones and he suspects Russia was behind the attacks.

blocks.text: A merchant ship has sunk after drones hit two vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.
He indicated Russia was suspected of the attacks and that he had called in its ambassador.

One of the ships went down 17 nautical miles (31km) east of Krapets and one crew member was saved, he said. The other, Ukrainian-owned vessel was hit by three drones 18 nautical miles from the town of Byala and all 15 crew were rescued, he added.

The drone attacks come a week after two other commercial ships were hit by sea and aerial drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. One of the ships, the Alfa Watan, sank and all 10 crew, including nine Syrians, are presumed dead.

Radev convened an emergency meeting on Tuesday and said he had summoned Russian envoy Eleonora Mitrofanova. Although there was no conclusive evidence of blame on "either side... the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation", he said.

Bulgaria is a Nato member and the prime minister said he would speak shortly to secretary general Mark Rutte. Radev had earlier asked Nato and the EU for technical assistance in investigating the 6 October attacks, indicating it was unclear whether Russia and Ukraine were behind them.
Radev came to office during the summer and has since rejected suggestions that he is "pro-Russian".

Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for the latest attacks and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke on Tuesday of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".
Russia's military has not publicly commented on the issue. It has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the Black Sea, particularly the western side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
The same day that two ships were targeted off Bulgaria last week, Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.
Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports - and cited attacks in the ports of Mykolaiv and Chornomorsk last week, along with one in the Black Sea.
However, Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.
Meeting with his security chiefs on Tuesday, Bulgaria's prime minister said: "Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable".

Radev identified one of the hit vessels as the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, which is registered in Ukraine's Odesa, saying that five its crew members were being treated for minor injuries. He gave no further details about the vessel that had sunk.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said "Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters... once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea.
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength," he added.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
