articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Tuesday referred its fact-finding investigation report on Vice President Sara Duterte"s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) to the…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 4:48pm

The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Tuesday referred its fact-finding investigation report on Vice President Sara Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) to the Ombudsman for evaluation and appropriate action.
According to GMA News’ Mav Gonzales, the investigation compared the Vice President’s SALN in 2024-2025 to the certified true copies of land titles obtained from the Land Registration Authority (LRA).

“The Bureau refers the matter to your Office, as the constitutional body with primary jurisdiction over public corruption under Article XI of the 1987 Constitution and Section 15 (1) of Republic Act No. 6770. The NBI stands ready to provide further records and to present its agents as witnesses should your Office require them,” the letter to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla read.
Along with the results of the investigation, the NBI also submitted the following documents to the Office of the Ombudsman:

items: Vice President Sara Duterte’s SALN for 2024-2025
14 LRA verified map location
22 land titles for 14 properties declared in the SALN
Surveillance photos and videos

blocks.text: The NBI is also investigating properties being linked to Duterte and her family amid allegations of cash deliveries by a dismissed police officer.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag said ex-cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.’s affidavit pointed to a pattern of “land banking” among properties linked to the family of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco, which the bureau is now examining in connection with some members of the Duterte family.
However, Davao lawmaker Paolo Duterte, the Vice President’s brother, challenged Matibag to establish the facts and present evidence to support his allegations.
Sara Duterte has denied ownership of the said properties.

In the impeachment trial of the Vice President, the impeachment court discussed the alleged unexplained wealth of Duterte, which includes the properties that she and her husband, Manases Carpio, own. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits
articles.summary: Germany long resisted tougher action against China because of retaliation fears. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin and Paris to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect…

image.caption: Germany and France are pushing for stronger EU trade defense tools amid rising Chinese competitionImage: DW

blocks.text: Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's unfair trade practices.
In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.

Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.
Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."
China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.
The cost of standing still

Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."
Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.
Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.

Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.
Why Berlin's China policy is changing

German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.

Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.

blocks.caption: VW, Audi and Porsche have announced workforce reductions totaling tens of thousands of jobs as the industry undergoes a huge transformationImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.

"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."
Industry pressure grows for trade defenses

Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:
"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.
According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.

While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.
Business groups question industrial policy proposals
The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, is meant to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.
Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.
How to dismantle China's stranglehold on raw materials?

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."

Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on the number of hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.
EU weights additional trade measures

Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half.
That could affect several millions vehicle exports from China to the EU over the next few years, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.

blocks.caption: Amid intense Chinese rivalry, the EU says it wants to restore industrial production in EuropeImage: Torsten Krüger/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.

MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion, versus $172 billion to the US.
This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.
"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

articles.title: Drones hit ships in Black Sea, sinking 1 and prompting rescue, Bulgaria says
articles.summary: Drones struck two ships in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.

image.caption: Rescued crew members from a ship that was damaged in a drone attack in the Black Sea are taken away in an ambulance in Varna, Bulgaria on Tuesday. (Bulphoto Agency/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Drones struck two ships in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
Bulgarian PM calls attacks 'absolutely unacceptable,' seeks NATO and European Union assistance
Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from one ship, the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries, Radev said in a video posted to social media.
The crew, which included seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijan citizens, reported the ship's deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones.

One crew member from the sunken vessel was rescued, Radev added, without providing details about the others aboard. The strikes on the two ships occurred 29 and 27.5 kilometres from the Bulgarian coast.

items: The Black Sea is the most dangerous it's been since the start of Russia’s war. And it's choking global grain

blocks.text: During an emergency meeting of Bulgaria's Security Council on Tuesday, Radev called the attacks "absolutely unacceptable" and said Bulgaria was seeking NATO and European Union assistance.
Crew members from a ship damaged in an earlier drone attack in the Black Sea on Oct. 6 disembark from a Bulgarian border police vessel in Varna, Bulgaria. (Petko Momchilov/Reuters)

While authorities do not possess clear evidence on who was responsible for the drone attacks, "logic, as I have already stated, indicates that the result is in favour of the Russian Federation," Radev said.

The attacks come exactly a week after sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew from a Pulau-flagged vessel.

items: Crew of ship missing after drone attacks on 2 commercial vessels in Black Sea near Bulgaria

blocks.text: Ukraine's military did not conduct any operations near the locations of last week's drone strikes, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who pointed the finger at Russia.

A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, pictured on Oct. 7, called Tuesday's drone strikes "absolutely unacceptable." (Hristo Vladev/NurPhoto/Getty Images)
Russia did not immediately comment on Tuesday's incident.
Radev said he would summon the Russian ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, for a conversation Tuesday.

articles.title: Impeach court grants prosecution bid to drop 3 of 4 charges vs VP Sara
articles.summary: The withdrawal is a major scaling back of the impeachment case, as the dropped charges included two of the most prominent allegations against Duterte.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 4:42pm

MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors on Tuesday, October 13, dropped three of the four impeachment charges against Vice President Sara Duterte, including the charges over alleged misuse of confidential funds and an alleged assassination plot.

The Senate impeachment court, through presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero, accepted the withdrawal of Articles I, III and IV, leaving Duterte’s trial to proceed on a single charge of unexplained wealth (Article II). Prosecutors have not had their chance to present Article III (bribery) and have also dropped that charge.

“Today, the prosecution respectfully manifests that it will no longer pursue three of them,” lead prosecutor Rep. Jinky Luistro told the court. “It will stand on one, and that is article two on unexplained wealth.”

This means none of the three withdrawn charges will be put to a vote. Now, Duterte can only be acquitted or convicted based solely on Article II, which accuses her of unexplained and undeclared wealth.

The withdrawal is a major scaling back of the impeachment case, as the dropped charges included two of the most prominent allegations against Duterte: the alleged misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds, and alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez. Prosecutors had already presented over a dozen witnesses on those two charges combined since July.

Dropping these articles means the prosecutors are now fully staking their case on the unexplained wealth charge against Duterte. Broken down, this article encompasses three matters: unexplained wealth, violations involving the SALN, and unlawful business interests.
Duterte will not get to rebut the dropped charges in court with her own evidence, since Escudero ruled that her defense will present evidence only on the remaining charge.

Luistro called the move to focus on just one article “the most judicious course,” saying a narrower case would spare the court from weighing evidence and objections on all four charges. She cited public impatience with a case she said began in 2024, and the Senate’s pending hearings on the 2027 national budget. She said the prosecution still considers all four charges “equally strong.”

In Escudero's extended ruling, the court ruled that Article I and Article IV were dropped with prejudice, meaning it cannot be brought against Duterte again during her current term in an impeachment trial.
“Having elected to withdraw the articles after resting its case, the prosecution must therefore accept the legal consequences of that withdrawal,” Escudero said.
The third dropped charge, on bribery in the Department of Education, could be refiled in the future because prosecutors withdrew it before presenting any evidence.

The court also lifted the restrictions on making public statements (known as Rule 18 or the sub judice rule) for Articles I, III, and IV. This means that both the prosecution and the defense can speak of the three allegations outside of the impeachment trial.

“Upon the effectivity of this order, the separate merits of Articles I, III, and IV are no longer pending for adjudication. Accordingly, the prosecutors, the respondent, their respective counsels, and witnesses may publicly address, explain, and respond to any matter contained in those withdrawn articles,” Escudero said.
With only Article II left for the defense to present its evidence for, the trial would likely finish well before the end of the year.
Defense strongly objects

The defense’s strongly worded objection, through lead counsel Sheila Sison, hit the court for a ruling that limits Duterte’s defense to the one remaining charge while lifting the gag on public discussion of the three dropped articles.
Sison warned that the second part would open “a free-for-all type of accusing the respondent anywhere and everywhere.”

“[The prosecution] presented their evidence. The court allowed them time, gave them opportunity, gave them platform, but now since they withdrew, your vice president can no longer speak or defend herself from those allegations,” Sison said. “We find that not only a bit unfair, I would say it’s completely unfair.”

She said the lifting of the sub judice rule, which bars parties from publicly discussing a pending case, was “not even a relaxation but what seems to be an entire abandonment of rule 18.” She added that “there should not be any single instance or occasion that this should be abandoned in the middle of trial.”
However, Escudero defended his ruling and reminded the defense that lifting Rule 18 for the three dropped articles would give Duterte the chance to defend herself out of court.

"The reason behind the relaxing of Rule 18 was more to afford the respondent to respond in the manner she may deem fit both in this courtroom, subject to the objections and ruling of the court, and outside," he said.

"The last thing I want for anyone to say when they leave this courtroom is, ‘Hindi na nga pinayagan sumagot sa loob ng hukuman, hindi pa pinayagan sumagot sa labas.’ Then I’d rather have the rule allow them to speak rather than not allow them to speak. Let that be the position at rest than the opposite,” he said.
Escudero deferred action on the defense’s objection to lifting the sub judice rule to give Duterte’s lawyers time to consult the vice president herself.

Defense panel spokesperson Michael Poa also cited an existing gag order issued by a regional trial court in connection with the grave threats case, which would severely limit their ability to speak of the case in public.
Shortened timetable
The prosecution must file its formal offer of evidence on Article II “within 10 days from today or until October 23,” Escudero ordered.
The defense has 10 days from receipt to file its comments and objections.
Duterte “shall have 26 calendar days from today within which to prepare for her presentation of evidence in chief" for Article II, with the defense’s presentation starting November 9.
The impeachment court will have about a three-week break after today before resuming the trial.

Escudero said the court will lose eight trial dates in November to budget hearings, an ASEAN-related break and holidays. The court set trial days on November 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 19, 20 and 23. Some of those dates are split with Senate sessions or shortened, and December dates will be set in early November.

articles.title: LIVE: ICC fourth status conference for ex-president Rodrigo Duterte
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court is holding the fourth status conference in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte on Tuesday, October 13.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 4:42pm
MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court is holding the fourth status conference in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte on Tuesday, October 13.
Duterte appears before the ICC Trial Chamber III as it discusses preparations for his trial, which is scheduled to begin on November 30.
The chamber is expected to discuss the trial schedule, including the time allotted for opening statements and the first block of evidence to be presented in December.

The parties will also discuss the prosecution’s list of witnesses and the number of hours it will need to present its case, as well as the estimated time needed by the defense and the victims’ common legal representative.
Other matters include the prosecution’s list of evidence, disclosure requirements, the defense’s submissions on its readiness for trial and requests for protective measures.

The status conference comes after the ICC ruled that Duterte is fit to stand trial. The tribunal’s decision, made public on October 8, cleared the way for the trial to proceed as scheduled on November 30.

The case stems from the ICC’s investigation into alleged crimes against humanity linked to killings during Duterte’s anti-drug campaign. Prosecutors have charged him with three counts of crimes against humanity involving alleged murders and attempted murders committed in the Philippines between November 2011 and March 2019.
Duterte was arrested in Manila in March 2025 and surrendered to the ICC on March 12, 2025. He remains detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen, The Hague, the Netherlands.

articles.title: Ex-president named leader of new DR Congo rebel coalition
articles.summary: Joseph Kabila had previously denied having links to the M23 rebels, which control much of eastern DR Congo.

blocks.text: Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has been named the leader of a new rebel coalition seeking to oust the government.

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it aimed to coordinate "resistance forces" to end "tyranny" in Democratic Republic of Congo and would pursue the goal "by all means, including force".

Its unveiling on Monday is the clearest indication so far of Kabila's direct involvement in an armed movement a year after he was sentenced to death in absentia for treason. He had previously denied having links to the M23 rebel group.
The Congolese government has not commented.
The coalition was announced at a press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma, the largest city in eastern DR Congo, which has been under the control of the M23 since last year.

M23 leader Sultani Makenga will serve as one of Kabila's four deputies in the new movement. The other three also come from the AFC-M23 alliance which last year seized much of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo.
The announcement of the new group comes days after Kabila delivered an address in which he said he would set out how Congolese people should act to "rescue" their country.
On Friday, Kabila accused President Félix Tshisekedi's government of disregarding proposals he had put forward last year, including some aimed at ending the conflict in eastern DR Congo.

Kabila also accused the government of undermining constitutional rule, mismanaging the economy and failing to improve security. He further alleged arbitrary arrests of political opponents and military officers.
The government has not publicly responded to those claims.
Kabila, 55, ruled DR Congo from 2001 until January 2019, when Tshisekedi took office following a disputed election.
The former president had remained largely out of public view for several years but has become increasingly critical of his successor's administration.
The formation of the new coalition comes at an uncertain time in a country that has been wracked by violence for decades.
More than 100 militia groups are active in eastern DR Congo amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources.
Tshisekedi's second term ends in 2028 but in May he said that elections, which are due then, may not be held because of the conflict.
He also hinted that he may seek re-election for a third term "if the people want".
The parliament has since passed a bill that could pave the way for a referendum that could remove the constitution's two-term limit.
Last month, authorities clashed with protesters holding demonstrations in the capital against the proposed changes.

articles.title: UK shoppers seek deals as grocery price inflation rises again
articles.summary: Supermarkets use special offers to draw in sales, while more people buy Halloween products early this year

blocks.text: UK grocery price inflation has edged up again as shoppers lean on special offers to keep their costs in check, new figures show.
Supermarket prices were 2.5% higher than last year in the four weeks to 4 October, up from 2.3% last month, data from Worldpanel by Numerator shows.

Spending on promotions over the last month was up by more than £250m compared with last year – with special offers remaining an important tool for shoppers hoping to keep their grocery bills in check, or to make pricier items and larger packs more affordable, Worldpanel said.

Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel, said: “With the autumn budget fast approaching, the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on the minds of shoppers. And the cost of filling up a car is only adding to the pressure on household budgets.
“More than half tell us they’re very or extremely worried about petrol prices, and almost one in three say it’s already taking a real toll on their finances.
“Until the chancellor sets out his plans, we expect that caution to carry on showing up at the till, with shoppers leaning more heavily on promotions to keep their grocery spend under control.”
However, in some good news for households preparing for Halloween, like-for-like chocolate confectionery prices are 3% lower than a year ago.

About 1.2 million households bought a pumpkin over the latest four weeks – an increase of 10% compared with the same time last year, while more than 250,000 households purchased a pumpkin spice coffee.
McKevitt added: “Halloween and Christmas are two of the most important moments of the year for chocolate confectionery, so falling prices will be welcome news for shoppers and retailers alike.

“After the double-digit increases of 2025, a 3% drop won’t fully reverse what consumers have paid in recent months, but it should help ease some of the pressure on household budgets as the festive season approaches.”
Lidl led in market share gains over the 12 weeks to 4 October, climbing to 8.6% on the back of a 7.1% increase in sales driven by fruit, vegetables and wine.

Sales at Ocado increased by 12.4%, outpacing overall online sales at 5.5%.
Spending through the tills was 1% higher at Tesco and 1.3% higher at Sainsbury’s, with the two retailers holding 27.8% and 15.2% of the market respectively.
Asda’s share now stands at 11.5%, while Aldi now holds 10.5% of the market, with sales at the discounter up 0.4% year on year.

articles.title: Marcos to media: Disagreement does not make us adversaries
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. said on Tuesday that disagreements between the government and the media do not make them adversaries, stressing that their relationship should be anchored on…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 4:16pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. said on Tuesday that disagreements between the government and the media do not make them adversaries, stressing that their relationship should be anchored on mutual respect and open dialogue.

Marcos made the remarks during the oath-taking of officers of three accredited media organizations at Malacañang: the Malacañang Press Corps (MPC), the Malacañang Cameramen Association (MCA) and the Presidential Photojournalists Association (PPA).

“The press has its own role to play in any democracy. And of course, we do not always agree on certain things, but that does not make us adversaries. I always see it as a partnership between both the media practitioners and those of us who are holding office because, after all, we all serve the public,” Marcos said.

“Therefore, our relationship remains grounded in mutual respect and open dialogue. And it is the only way that I know to have a productive and constructive relationship between the practitioners in the media and those of us who are in office,” he added.
Marcos recognized GMA News reporter Ivan Mayrina, MPC president, as well as MCA president Rolly Demawalo and PPA president Noel Pabalate.
He said the media's role has become even more critical amid the spread of disinformation and the growing use of artificial intelligence.

“Whether through reports, photographs, videos, your work helps Filipinos to understand the events and to know how these events affect their lives and the decisions that they will have to make for themselves in light of the context that you make and offer,” Marcos said.
The administration is also working to combat disinformation through its “Oplan Kontra Fake News” initiative.
Marcos said his administration was likewise committed to protecting journalists and other media workers from threats and violence.

“This administration remains committed to ensuring that our reporters, our photojournalists and cameramen can perform their duties freely, safely and without fear of intimidation or violence from anywhere,” he said.

The President also cited the work of the Presidential Task Force on Media Security in protecting journalists, including the establishment of media monitoring centers during the Bangsamoro parliamentary elections.— MCG, GMA News

blocks.text: The ministers get asked about Trump’s diesel deal with Putin.
They don’t really offer any hot takes on this.
Germany’s Wadephul says that Europe needs to keep talking to Trump, and keep imposing sanctions on Russia.
Poland’s Sikorski makes a domestic point, putting pressure on Poland’s Maga-friendly president Karol Nawrocki to intervene with Trump directly.
Norway’s Espen Barth Eide also focuses on Europe’s resolve, more than anything else.
By the way, you can watch the Warsaw Security Forum panel with Barth Eide, Miliband, Sikorski, and Wadephul here.
'We are facing a really testing period' on Ukraine, Russian hybrid warfare, UK's Miliband says
UK’s Miliband is next.

He draws on his family’s history, saying his mother found refuge in Warsaw during the second world war, and he had “an amazing visit” to the Jewish Historical Institute this morning where he saw documents about his family’s history.
“It is a reminder of what war means for the ravaging of people’s lives and the uprooting of people’s lives.”
But he then moves on to Ukraine as he says:

“I think our job is not to be analysts, but to lead. We are four and a half years into this warm and the truth is that our resolve is being tested. Our resolve is being tested as far as Ukraine is concerned, resolve is being tested with Russian hybrid warfare, and our job is to stop and to respond. I feel a sense of confidence, but I don’t think we can be complacent at all. We are facing a really testing period. Putin is not winning this war, but him not winning is not good enough for us yet. And therefore what we do in the coming months, whether it is on sanctions, continuing to increase the pressure on Russia, whether it is the fiscal support for Ukraine, whether it’s defensive support for Ukraine, all of this really, really matters, and it matters morally, and it matters also to European security.”
Support for Ukraine over the coming winter is critical, EU ministers say
The four ministers are speaking now.
Poland’s Sikorski says he “regrets” that Europe “wasted” the first two years of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and is only now “catching up” when it comes to rearmaments.

“By the end of the decade, we will have a combined army, even just around the Baltic and the Eastern flank, that Putin would be crazy to attack. But if that is our calendar, that would be too late for Ukraine,” he says.
He says it’s critical to sustain Ukraine through the coming winter.
Germany’s Wadephul says Europe is “more united than we were at the beginning of the war,” and “have more capabilities.”
“The winter will be challenging, but we know what to do.”
Over in Warsaw, Poland’s parliament speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty is beginning his opening speech telling the audience that Europe is “at the turning point” of “civilisational” significance.
Addressing the Warsaw Security Forum, he says “for those who have any doubts that the president of the Russian Federation is a murderer and aggressor, and Ukraine is a victim.”
He says “it has to be said: there is no free Poland and free Europe, without a free Ukraine.”

Just as he says it, Poland issues a (now fairly routine) emergency alert to residents of a south-eastern region neighbouring Ukraine, putting them on high alert because of Russian strikes across the border.
The foreign ministers of Britain, Germany, Poland and Norway should be up on the main stage shortly.
Morning opening: Two ships hit by drones off Bulgarian coast

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Drones of unknown origin struck two ships in the Black Sea off Bulgaria this morning, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations, the country’s prime minister Rumen Radev said.

blocks.caption: Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev addresses the media following an incident in Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone last week. Photograph: Spasiyana Sergieva/Reuters

blocks.text: Only one person was rescued from the sunken vessel, and 15 people were picked up from the other one.
The attack comes exactly a week after a similar incident in which one ship sank with its crew on board, and the other one was evacuated, with 18 people rescued.
PM Radev said the attacks were “absolutely unacceptable,” and said he would seek assistance from Nato and the European Union.
He said that while there is no “clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility” yet, “the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.”
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said “the Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine.”

“This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea. We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable.”

The incident comes amid growing fears about Russia’s war against Ukraine and as several European foreign ministers meet at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, including Britain’s Ed Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul, and Ukraine’s Andrii Sybiha.
I will monitor their comments and bring you the top lines.
Separately, the French high school protests are expected to intensify today after key groups called for “a day of mobilisation” across the country.
Over in Spain, the Spanish royals are expected to visit the autonomous city of Ceuta in northern Africa, which continues to see its every day’s life disrupted by the migration crisis.

In Sweden, the Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson is due to report back on the progress of her talks on government formation today. But early reports suggest she does not quite have everything lined up yet, and the process is likely to take more time.

Finally, in the Vatican, Pope Leo is expected to be hospitalised today to remove a lung nodule discovered in his body to test it if the lesion is malignant. He is likely to stay there for about a week.
So, lots for us to cover. I will bring you all the key lines here.
It’s Monday, 13 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Andy Burnham will take Britain back into European Union, Neil Kinnock claims – UK politics live
articles.summary: Former Labour leader says he believes the prime minister has an ‘authentic commitment’ to taking the UK back into the EU

blocks.text: Good morning. In his long statement to MPs yesterday, Andy Burnham was evasive when asked whether he wanted his planned renegotiation of Britain’s relationship with the EU to result in a Labour-led government, after the next election, rejoining. In response to one question about this, Burnham told a Tory MP he was “getting way ahead of himself” with the question. But one well-placed observer is not being so coy.

Neil Kinnock, the former Labour leader and one of three people Burnham has named as his political mentors, has given an interview to la Repubblica, the Italian newspaper. He told it that he believes Burnham does want to, and will, take the UK back into the EU.
Kinnock said: “Andy makes the declaration of his determination to change the relationship, and it’s obvious that his objective is to join again.”
Asked again if he thought Burnham would be the person to take the UK back into the EU, Kinnock replied:

double quotation markYes, sure, sure, sure. His commitment is authentic. He really does understand from the grassroots up why restoring what I think of as normality in our continent is vital for every party economically, politically, culturally, all in security terms, and is able to articulate it in language that people can understand. So yeah, he is definitely.
Asked about Burnham playing down his desire to revisit the referendum result during the Makerfield byelection campaign, Kinnock claimed this was just a matter of deciding when to have this debate.

double quotation markAndy’s not changed direction. He’s always been a committed pro-European. In the byelection, he rightly didn’t make a noise about it. That’s tomorrow’s debate. Simply because the byelection wasn’t about Europe. It was about winning Makerfield in order to enable him to become leader of the party. That’s all it was about.

Kinnock was interviewed by Antonello Guerrera who asked how, as someone who inherited a leftwing party and dragged it to the right, Kinnock felt about a sucessor taking Labour to the left. Kinnock said he thought Burnham’s approach was right.

double quotation markIt’s common sense. It’s not left and right. Andy’s view of the engagement of the state is about what Winston Churchill did in the 1950s, and I don’t remember Churchill being thought of as on the left. Andy’s a socialist, but he’s a very common-sense socialist. He’s very rational. He’s cool, not just with his dark blue T-shirt, but in his thinking, and he’s advanced a hell of a lot in the last 10–12 years in terms of his understanding of the absolute importance of utility, of usefulness in politics. That’s what puts us, basically, he and I, on the same spot. Of course he’s on the left. I’m on the left. We’re socialists, but we are prompted by the usefulness of the application of ideas.

We have got a lobby briefing later and no doubt No 10 will clarify that its understanding of Burnham’s position on rejoining the EU is not quite the same as Kinnock’s. Kinnock is a former vice president of the European Commission, and an ardent pro-European, and perhaps there is some wishful thinking in what he says. But he is also a good friend of Burnham, and an astute observer of Labour politics. You will have to decide for yourself if he is right.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet.
Morning: Burnham attends meetings with business leaders in No 10.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: MPs debate the remaining stages of the courts and tribunals bill.
3pm: Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, gives evidence to the Commons defence committee.
5pm: Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, attends the regular weekly meeting of Lib Dem MPs, after two frontbenchers stood down amid concerns about his leadership.
Also today, another round of prisoner releases is happening under the prisoner early release scheme in England.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Palace: VP Sara’s statement means she is ‘really into business with China’
articles.summary: Castro said Duterte should listen first before stirring any controversy, adding that the vice president reacted and responded to Marcos without reviewing his actual statement.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 4:13pm
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives before the start of the impeachment trial at the Senate of the Philippines in Pasay, Metro Manila on July 7, 2026.
Noel Celis, pool / AFP

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang said Vice President Sara Duterte’s response to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s earlier remarks about her alleged China-linked funds appeared to indicate that she may indeed be involved in business dealings with China.
“With that statement of the vice president, it means she is really into business with China,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said at a press briefing on Tuesday, October 13.

The recent exchange of remarks between Malacañang and the vice president started when Marcos commented on claims that Cale88 Foods Corp., a firm linked to Duterte and her husband, lawyer Mans Carpio, received at least P319 million in remittances from China and Hong Kong.
Marcos said on October 11 that the claims about the Chinese money constitute a national security threat “at the highest level” if proven true.

In response, Duterte said in a press briefing on Monday, October 12, during the sidelines of the 91st anniversary celebration of the Office of the Vice President that Marcos’ comment was concerning, especially for Filipino businesses with deals with China, as it implied a prohibition against such deals.

"Parang sinasabi niya na 'yung mga nagnenegosyo o mayroong trade sa China ay threat din sa bansa," Duterte said. "So, ano ba talaga? Bawal ba talaga magnegosyo with China kasi it's a national security risk?"

(It was as if he was saying that those who have business deals or trades with China are also threats to the country. So, what is it? Is it really prohibited to do business with China kasi it's a national security risk?)
‘No prohibitions vs China business deals’
Castro said Duterte should listen first before stirring any controversy, adding that the vice president reacted and responded to Marcos without reviewing his actual statement.
The Palace spokesperson clarified that, based on what the president said, the alleged China-linked funds could only be considered a “threat” once supported by evidence.
“Huwag agad mag-react nang hindi binabasa kung ano mismo ang salita ng pangulo dahil ang iyong magiging mensahe ay pawang kasinungalingan o pawang hindi relevant dahil mali.
"Ang sabi ng pangulo kung may ebidensya, ito ay makukunsiderang national threat — kung,” Castro said, emphasizing the conditional nature of the statement.

(Do not react immediately without reading the actual words of the president because your message will be purely false, or purely irrelevant, because it is wrong. The president said if there’s evidence, it could be considered a national threat — if.)

Castro also stressed that Marcos did not mention anything about banning business deals with China in his comment on the matter, saying the Philippine government itself has diplomatic deals with the country.
“Hindi pwedeng sabihin na dinemonize ang China. There is no prohibition in dealing with China in relation to trade and investment,” Castro said. (They can’t say China was demonized.)

articles.title: Chiz Escudero bares Sara Duterte impeachment trial schedule for November
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday released the new schedule of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte for next month.

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 4:11pm
The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday released the new schedule of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte for next month.
According to presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero, the impeachment court shall hold trial in the following dates:

items: November 9: Court will convene at 10 a.m., the Senate will have a session in the afternoon and resume the trial after the session
November 10: Whole day, from 10 a.m. onwards
November 11: Court will convene at 10 a.m., the Senate may conduct session in the afternoon as needed
November 12: Whole day, from 10 a.m. onwards
November 13: Whole day, from 10 a.m. onwards
November 19: Whole day, from 10 a.m. onwards
November 20: Whole day, from 10 a.m. onwards
November 23: From 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. only

blocks.text: “The Court is presently ahead of its projected trial schedule under the pre-trial order given the schedule proposed for the presentation of prosecution evidence by 20 trial days as of today because of our whole day hearings,” Escudero said.

“However, due to the scheduled recess of about three weeks, we will only be ahead by three trial days by November 9. And considering the budget hearings, the ASEAN-related break, and other holidays, eight available trial days will be lost in the month of November,” he added.
The presiding officer said the court shall decide on the impeachment schedule in December as the case may be, hopefully at the beginning of November to give the parties adequate time. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: 125 years of Thomas Mann's 'Buddenbrooks'
articles.summary: This over 1,000-page masterpiece offers a panoramic view of society in the 19th century and exposes the collapse of a merchant family: unrecognized sons, disillusioned daughters and the loss of…

image.caption: Thomas MannImage: picture-alliance/dpa

blocks.text: Who would have imagined it in the beginning? A 26-year-old man without a high school diploma, but greatly ambitious, writes a two-pound book with a melancholy undertone. "I'm not exactly delighted," his publisher initially responded. But he ended up publishing the novel anyway, more out of goodwill than conviction. And the rest is history.

For many, Thomas Mann's Buddenbrooks is considered THE German social novel. It is indeed a classic, and one that garnered the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. Global fame, an international best-seller, and required reading for many German students. Anyone who mentions Thomas Mann thinks of Buddenbrooks in the same breath. Why is that?
Life as a literary model
Does the explanation lie in the autobiographical connections between the work and the author?

Thomas Mann was born in Lübeck to a merchant family, but his artistic aspirations did not fit in well in the middle-class mainstream. This struggle inspired Mann's first work. The inability of this sensitive bohemian to carry on the family's time-honored business after the death of his father was sniffed at and derided.
'Buddenbrooks' by Thomas Mann

Reflecting the situation of his novel's character Hanno, Mann had a privileged life in a wealthy family, but one that was at risk of collapse. The aspiring novelist also had to withstand disappointing the expectations of others. He was forced to defend his dream of an artistic life. Yet as much as he was inspired by real life, he forcefully altered these biographical details to place his unique literary mark on his writing.
Appearance over substance

But does that really matter in light of people who choose not to make the distinction between an author's life and his work? Even though the name "Lübeck" does not appear in the novel, citizens there felt markedly insulted after the publication of Buddenbrooks in 1901.
That likely lies in the fact that the image the author portrayed was not one of an idyllic northern German city, but one of a place that had difficulty blending tradition with modernity.

blocks.caption: People were initially shocked over 'Buddenbrooks' in Lübeck, but now, Thomas Mann's statue stands tall in the cityImage: picture alliance/AP

blocks.text: This contradiction is also seen in each of the figures in the novel. Nothing is like it appears. Mann lays down this foundation of this skepticism from the very beginning, in a scene taking place on a very ordinary Thursday in October 1835. The Buddenbrook family comes together for their ordinary late lunch.

"There they all sat, on heavy, high-backed chairs, consuming good heavy food from good silver plates, drinking full-bodied wines and expressing their views freely on all subjects. When they began to talk shop, they slipped unconsciously more and more into dialect, and used the clumsy but comfortable idioms that seemed to embody to them the business efficiency and the easy well-being of their community. Sometimes they even used an over-drawn pronunciation by way of making fun of themselves and each other, and relished their clipped phrases and exaggerated vowels with the same heartiness they did their food."
Failing grandly

There sits the leader of the family company, Johann Buddenbrook the Elder, and his wife, his son and counsel Jean, along with his family. The grandchildren are also there: Tony the dreamer, the quarrelsome rebel Christian, and Thomas, the eldest grandchild.

It is Thomas who is supposed to later take on the responsibility of continuing the family tradition, regardless of the cost. Mann weaves his narrative work starting with this main family, and then across several generations.

But appearances in the family are deceptive. The reader senses it's all headed toward a downfall. The new house is taken over from a family that was once as illustrious as the Buddenbrooks, but faced financial ruin and had to leave.
Johann and his family aim to make a better go of it. They make decisions on what is demanded economically, but fail — financially, interpersonally, and mentally.

Tony and Thomas end up falling in love with people not befitting their social standing, but do not have the courage to stand up to their parents. They enter marriages of convenience, yet it is these partnerships that paradoxically set disaster in motion.
Language as a mirror

From an early age, Thomas Mann was influenced by Schopenhauer's pessimistic notion of the will being a blind force at work in the world. Thus, there is likewise no escape for the Buddenbrooks. They speak of emotions and morality, yet it is money and economics that steer the ship. Failure, decline and even death seem to be the only viable outcome.

Mann also punctuates this hopelessness in a stylistic manner, by consistently repeating entire passages word for word, or evoking motifs such as the family registry or the estate in all their various forms.

blocks.caption: Heinrich Breloer turned the novel into a film in 2008 Image: picture-alliance/dpa/Bavaria Film/S. Falke

blocks.text: The extent of this demise appears linguistically molded and exaggerated. The Buddenbrooks, this proud north German family of refinement, actually speaks the vernacular studded with empty French expressions. "Je, den Düwel ook, c'est la question, ma très chère demoiselle!"

The lowly servants, the courtesans, and the demi-monde: all of them speak the language of the street, raw and unpolished. In a virtuoso manner, Thomas Mann orchestrated this mass of voices into a panorama of society in the 19th century. The snobbishness on the part of the Buddenbrooks thus appears as a relic of a long lost time. It's a symbol of their inability to adapt to change and place their faith in progress.
Stuffy husbands and anxious sons

Yet the fact that this extensive work spanning several generations does not get weighed down by aesthetic excess is purely due to Mann's brilliance as an author. He is able to bring every one of his numerous characters to life in words. Life that is full of complexity, contradictions and ambiguities. Some of these characters accompany the reader page for page; others appear only briefly.

And yet one begins to contemplate how someone like Grünlich could become a dodgy, unscrupulous husband and catches oneself wanting to chase the fearful Hanno out of the music conservatory and yell to him: "Go, throw yourself into life! You are not a failure." It is precisely this empathy that spurs one on to read through the night and prompts one to chuckle at all the intricate sentences and philosophical digressions.
Thomas Mann: Buddenbrooks, Vintage Classics / Penguin Random House, (German title: Buddenbrooks, 1901). English translation: John E. Woods

Thomas Mann was born into a privileged Lübeck merchant family in 1875. He died in Zurich, Switzerland in 1955. "I am a townsman, a citizen, a child and a great-grandchild of German bourgeois society," the author once wrote about himself. Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 for his debut novel, Buddenbrooks. He also garnered numerous other prizes and honors for his extensive work, including Death in Venice (1911), The Magic Mountain (1924), and the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers (1933-1943). He emigrated to Switzerland in 1933, and to the US in 1938. From there, he made his famous radio commentaries in which he agitated against the Nazis. He returned to Switzerland in 1952.
This article was first published as part of the series 100 German must-reads.
