blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 4:05pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has appointed Social Security System (SSS) chief Robert Joseph Montes de Claro as the new secretary of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), replacing Henry Aguda.
While his reasons for quitting were not disclosed, Aguda resigned from the post in October following a controversy over the banning of online platform Discord.
“I have already signed the ad interim appointment of the new DICT secretary is Robert Joseph Montes de Claro," Marcos said during the oathtaking accredited media groups at the Palace.
"He is the current SSS president and CEO and he also, besides that, he also has a very strong background in terms of the digital economy, the digital world,” he added.
Marcos said that De Claro was also the Chair of the Information Technology Connection committee of the SSS, and he also represented the social pensioners in the Board of Trustees of UnionBank.
Speaking before the media, de Claro thanked the employees of the SSS and apologized for being unable to bid them a proper farewell.
Asked about the issue of banning social media platforms, de Claro said that the best cure was prevention.

“I’ll have a thorough review of all the projects, budgets, and procurement ng DICT, and I assure the public that over the next three months, there should be a clear-cut plan on how to take DICT on where it should be,” de Claro said. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: DOE: Visayas may face more red alerts in 2027 without sufficient backup systems
articles.summary: Energy officials say power barges and battery energy storage systems can address the imbalance in power supply and demand in the Visayas

blocks.text: RISK. Energy Secretary Sharon Garin says the Visayas grid is at risk of facing more red alerts if the government is unable to secure the necessary ancillary services to help balance the region's power demand and supply, on October 12, 2026.
Cebu Provincial Government
Energy officials say power barges and battery energy storage systems can address the imbalance in power supply and demand in the Visayas

items: Energy Secretary Sharon Garin warned that the Visayas could face more red alerts in 2027 if ancillary services procurement agreements for 250 megawatts of power reserves are not secured.
The region's coal-fired power plants are experiencing forced outages due to operational issues and increased energy demand, leading to overworking of the plants.
To stabilize the energy supply, the Department of Energy plans to implement battery energy storage systems and additional power plants, including coal, gas, and renewable sources, by 2028.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CEBU, Philippines – Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said on Monday, October 12, that the Visayas could face more red alerts in 2027 if the government is unable to secure ancillary services procurement agreements (ASPAs) for 250 megawatts of power reserves.
For months, major coal-fired power plants in Visayas have been on forced and unplanned outages due to operational damage, system failures, and the region’s growing energy demand.

“We overwork our coal power plants. Imbes na magmaintenance siya or dapat hindi siya 100%, talagang sinasagad natin kasi kulang ang supply (Instead of doing maintenance or it not operating at 100%, we’re really overworking it because the supply is lacking),” Garin said in an interview during a summit convening energy experts and officials in Cebu.

Data from the Department of Energy (DOE) as of April 30 showed that Visayas’ coal plants contribute at least 1,233 megawatts of dependable energy capacity of the existing 3,449 megawatts of dependable capacity in the region — a third of the region’s dependable power mix is coal-based.

In 2025, system peak demand in the Visayas had grown to 2,691 megawatts from 2,201 megawatts in 2020, according to DOE data. This presents a huge problem to power plants as they are forced to work overtime to meet the demand, exposing plants to high-stress and early deterioration.

To address this, Garin said that the Visayas should have its own set of ancillary services, particularly battery energy storage systems (BESS), to offset the lack of supply and keep plants operating at a stable capacity.

“The batteries will work more like a stabilizer para kung kailan kulang ang supply, tapos malaki ang demand, siya ang mag-susupply (so when there is a lack of supply, and the demand is great, this will be the one to supply),” Garin added.

As early as May 22, the DOE directed the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) to execute ASPAs for at least 250 megawatts of Visayas reserves. On October 5, the DOE called out the NGCP for failing to file the required ASPAs.

“The Visayas needed these reserves on the grid months ago. What was missing was timely execution. Delays in contracting left consumers with less protection when generating units unexpectedly went offline,” Garin said in the DOE’s October 5 press release.
As a system operator, it is the NGCP’s responsibility to balance the supply and demand of power to maintain the quality of electricity that flows through the grid.

Without the ASPAs, the DOE reported that red alerts could occur for at least 22 of the 52 weeks in 2027, around February to November. With the ASPAs, the number of weeks with red alerts could drop to only four weeks.
At present, the Visayas grid has 134 megawatts of dependable capacity from its BESS.

Garin shared, in a presentation on the Visayas energy road map during the Cebu summit, that they are expecting to put up at least 250 megawatts of BESS and deploy power barges — power plants installed on a barge — between 2026 and 2027.

But the reserves are only for the short term. In the long term, the DOE is hoping to increase the region’s energy supply with new base load plants that provide steady power. This, Garin said, would come in the form of coal, nuclear, diesel, and geothermal energy sources.

By 2028, the DOE expects 150 megawatts in baseload capacity from an expansion project of Therma Visayas Inc.’s coal-fired power plant in Toledo City. This project is not covered under the country’s moratorium on new coal-power projects.

Apart from the additional 150 megawatts, a 220-megawatt gas-based power plant in Cebu, and 470 megawatts from a renewable energy plant in Cebu and Bohol are set to be finished before the end of 2028. Panay Island is also expected to get a 220-megawatt gas-based power plant and a 135-megawatt baseload plant in the same year.
“We have a very fragile system but the good thing is we are already working on it to make it less fragile,” Garin said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Albay political commentator shot dead
articles.summary: Police face a blank wall on the October 12 shooting death of local political commentator Adrian Loterte in Albay

items: Local political commentator Adrian Nacion Loterte was shot and killed by unidentified gunmen in Daraga, Albay, while tending to his bakery.
The motive for the attack remains unclear, and police are investigating potential connections to Loterte's work in media and his political commentary.
Local officials and organizations condemned the violence, emphasizing the need for accountability and a thorough investigation into the killing.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
ALBAY, Philippines – Local political commentator Adrian Nacion Loterte was shot and killed by two still unidentified gunmen in Daraga town, Albay, on Monday afternoon, October 12.
According to an initial investigation by the Police Regional Office V, Loterte was tending to his bakery in a rented space in Barangay San Roque around 4:10 pm when the assailants attacked.
Loterte succumbed to four gunshot wounds – he was rushed to Daraga Doctors Hospital, where he was declared dead while undergoing treatment.
Police said the suspects, who were reportedly riding a white-and-black Honda Click motorcycle, fled toward neighboring Barangay Kimantong immediately after the shooting.

“The motive behind the incident remains undetermined. PRO-5 assures the public that all possible angles are being thoroughly investigated and that no effort will be spared in establishing the facts, determining the circumstances that led to the shooting, and bringing those responsible to justice,” the police said.

Authorities are conducting CCTV backtracking and footage analysis in coordination with the Albay Police Provincial Office Command Center to trace the suspects’ movements before and after the shooting.
“Available CCTV footage showing the suspects has also been disseminated to concerned police units to aid in their identification and support ongoing dragnet operations,” PRO-5 added.
Daraga Mayor Victor Perete condemned the attack, calling for a thorough and impartial investigation by the Philippine National Police (PNP).
“Those found responsible must be held accountable under the law. There must be no room for violence, intimidation, or impunity in our community,” Perete said in a statement.
“As we await verified developments, I appeal to the public to remain vigilant and responsible by refraining from spreading unverified information that could prejudice the investigation.”

Known as “Golden Boy,” Loterte was a news anchor for RBN News Television’s Rabas Cun Rabas and a blocktimer at DWIZ FM in Legazpi City. Both programs frequently aired commentary on local political issues.

Political tensions involving Loterte intensified in October 2025, when he filed a petition before the Commission on Elections seeking to cancel former Albay governor Noel Rosal’s certificate of candidacy.

Loterte alleged that Rosal had committed material misrepresentation and was ineligible to run following an Ombudsman ruling in 2024 ordering Rosal’s dismissal from service. Loterte had originally filed the complaint in 2022.
Rosal condemned the killing, emphasizing that political or personal grievances never justify violence to silence someone. He promised to expedite a thorough investigation to ensure justice.

“No disagreement warrants violence, and no difference in opinion, cause, or conviction can ever justify the unlawful taking of a human life,” Rosal said in a statement. “Political rivalry must never erase our shared humanity; personal grievances must not diminish the value we place on human life.”
AKO Bicol Representative Alfredo Garbin said differences in political views must be addressed with reasons and remedies, not bullets.
“Adrian Loterte is known in Albay for his hard-hitting commentaries on political and public affairs.
Whether one agrees or disagrees with his views, no individual should ever be subjected to violence for exercising the right to free expression,” Garbin said in a post.

Garbin said no journalist, broadcaster, commentator, or citizen should have their life endangered for speaking freely. He urged the police to investigate Loterte’s line of work as a potential motive for the crime.
“Authorities must determine whether this attack was connected to Loterte’s work as a media personality, without ruling out other possible motives until the evidence is established,” Garbin added.

Background checks on Loterte’s media affiliations show that RBN News’ Facebook page, created in 2017, contains no publicly available details about its ownership or official registration. The page has consistently posted updates featuring prominent local politicians, particularly Garbin and the AKO Bicol Party-list.
Meanwhile, DWIZ FM, which operates under Aliw Broadcasting Corporation, has a pending accreditation application with the Kapisanan ng mga Broadcaster ng Pilipinas (KBP).
“Loterte was last active as a member of KBP in 2019,” KBP-Albay confirmed.

Loterte was a known colleague and close friend of slain media practitioner Noel Bellen Samar, who was shot dead in Guinobatan, Albay, on October 20, 2025. Samar’s case also remains unsolved as of writing.
“Violence and intimidation must never be tolerated, and attacks against media practitioners and personalities must never be met with impunity,” KBP-Albay said in its statement of condemnation.

In 2018, Joey Llana, a reporter for Home Radio Legazpi, was also killed in Daraga after being ambushed and sustaining 14 gunshot wounds. (READ: Propaganda, attacks on journalists undermine press freedom in Bicol)

The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP)-Albay chapter reported that, from 2023 to October 2026, it had recorded more than four murder cases involving media practitioners, 17 cyber libel cases, and numerous incidents of intimidation, harassment, and red-tagging across the province. – Rappler.com

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Trillanes not cited in contempt by impeachment court
articles.summary: No credible reports or statements support the claim; the House’s lead prosecutor has also rejected calls for Trillanes to be cited in contempt for airing allegations against Duterte

blocks.text: Claim: Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV has been cited in contempt and faces possible arrest over his criticism of the Senate impeachment court in Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial.
Why we fact-checked this: Three separate videos carry versions of the claim.

The first, posted by “Pinas News Insider” on October 4, is titled, “Guilty ang hatol? (The verdict is ‘guilty’?) He should be cited in contempt and sent to Pasay City Jail – Jay Zonsa VP Sara Chiz.” It shows a photo of a press briefing by Senate impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol.
The second, posted by “PoliTalak” on the same day, is titled, “Sen Chiz Escudero sumabog na sa galit; harapang tinapos si Trillanes. Wala ng takas, himas rehas na?”
(Sen. Chiz Escudero exploded in anger, confronted Trillanes face to face, no escape, already behind bars?)
Text on its thumbnail reads, “Contempt na! Ikukulong na sa Senado! Bastos ka! Walang modo!”
(Already in contempt! He’ll be jailed at the Senate! You’re rude! No manners.)
The third, posted by “Pinas News Portal” and credited to “Banat By,” is titled, “Chiz galit na! Big ultimatum! Contempt na Trillanes!”
(Chiz is already angry! Big ultimatum! Trillanes is already cited in contempt!)
Overall, the three videos have garnered more than 67,000 views and 2,900 likes as of writing.

The facts: No contempt citation has been issued against Trillanes, and there is no credible report that presiding officer Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero or the impeachment court threatened to jail him.

The misleading videos surfaced after Trillanes held a press conference on October 2, where he presented findings from his own investigation into Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth, including claims that entities tied to the Vice President received hundreds of millions of pesos in funds from the “Chinese government and corporations.”
The former senator made these allegations after he was dropped from the prosecution’s witness list on October 1 upon his request.

Trillanes also took a swipe at Escudero, asking why he was not issued a subpoena for him to testify on charges of Duterte’s unexplained wealth. He said it was “clear” that he was “not welcome” at the impeachment court.

In response, Tongol called Trillanes’ claim a “baseless assumption.” Senate President Win Gatchalian and Senator Panfilo Lacson also clarified that the decision not to have Trillanes subpoenaed was reached by consensus among the senator-judges, not by Escudero alone.

The calls to cite Trillanes in contempt came from outside the impeachment court. Lawyer Jimmy Bondoc called for Trillanes to be cited for indirect contempt over his remarks against Escudero. But House lead prosecutor and Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville Luistro rejected the idea in an October 2 interview, noting that Trillanes is not a party to the impeachment trial and that his remarks were protected free speech.
Impeachment trial updates: On October 5, Escudero told the impeachment court not to be distracted by outside criticism, while acknowledging “high tensions” during the impeachment trial.

The House prosecution ended its presentation of evidence in Duterte’s trial on October 12, expressing confidence that the evidence could support her conviction. Meanwhile, Duterte’s defense panel will start the presentation of their evidence on November 9. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte) – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Ottawa wants to expand the oilsands, but the industry's wastewater problem will grow with it
articles.summary: The recent decision by Prime Minister Mark Carney to fast-track a new oil export pipeline to the West Coast is adding urgency for Ottawa to finally decide what to do with a long-standing…

image.caption: Scarecrows and air cannons are used to prevent birds from landing on tailings ponds in the oilsands region near Fort McMurray, Alta. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

blocks.text: The recent decision by Prime Minister Mark Carney to fast-track a new oil export pipeline to the West Coast is adding urgency for Ottawa to finally decide what to do with a long-standing environmental issue plaguing the oilsands in Northern Alberta — what to do with tailings ponds.
Oil output in the region is set to grow and the Alberta government wants to double the amount of crude production.

Yet, ever since the first oilsands mine was built about 60 years ago, the industry has been banned from releasing any water. As a result, large tailings ponds throughout the region are filled with decades worth of industrial mining wastewater. The fluid is toxic and harmful to wildlife. For those who live in the region, they fear the harmful health effects, in addition to the impact on the environment.

All day, every day, every few seconds, air cannons blast on the edge of the tailings ponds to help deter birds, ducks and other wildlife from the water, in addition to dozens of makeshift scarecrows dressed in overalls and hard hats.
The problem is as big as 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools or the area of the Island of Montreal under three metres of water.
An aerial view of a tailings pond, which holds mining wastewater and contains various contaminants. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
The amount of tailings fluid continues to increase after growing by 50 per cent over a 10-year period from 2014 to 2024, according to the Alberta Energy Regulator.

As tailings ponds fill up, the industry is urgently pushing for government regulations allowing for the fluid to be treated and then released. At the same time, some Indigenous leaders are calling for oilsands production to slow down until this issue is properly resolved.
Tailings ponds are at capacity and no one wants more of the storage lakes built, said Alberta's Environment Minister Grant Hunter, in an interview with CBC News in Fort McMurray.

"The solution isn't just to keep doing nothing and put our head in the sand. The solution is to actually prove out the science," he said. "We cannot say to industry, 'we want you to double production,' and then not give them the tools to be able to do proper treat-and-release."
Prime Minister Mark Carney announces the proposed Pacific Link pipeline will be fast-tracked during an event in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Oct. 1. (Todd Korol/Reuters)
Alberta's proposal

By the end of the year, the Alberta government plans to lay out exactly what quality standards have to be met for water to be released. Still, the waterways fall under federal jurisdiction, so it will be up to Ottawa to adopt those proposed regulations, suggest changes or keep the ban in place.

Companies insist they have the technology and expertise to treat tailings water. They just need the regulations to know what water quality standards have to be reached. Companies say they will never be able to properly clean up large amounts of land until the tailings ponds are addressed.

items: Mayors, First Nations chiefs in Alberta's oilsands region react tentatively to West Coast pipeline designation

blocks.text: "Treating and release is really critical to enabling the large-scale reclamation of these facilities," said Claire Greenwood, a vice-president with Suncor Energy, while speaking at a recent energy conference in Fort McMurray.

"These tailings facilities are not meant to be permanent parts of the landscape in the region. We have full intention of actually turning those tailings ponds into reclaimed sites. And so that's why we're looking for that treatment release."
The company rejected interview requests from CBC News and would not provide access to a water treatment demonstration facility near Fort McMurray.

From left: Suncor's Claire Greenwood, Imperial's Jessica Dillabough and Alberta Environment Minister Grant Hunter speak in favour of developing a treat-and-release policy for the industry, while speaking on a panel during the Oil Sands Expo in Fort McMurray on Sept. 16. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

If treat-and-release is allowed, the water would be pumped into the Athabasca River, which flows directly north from Fort McMurray and the oilsands region to several Indigenous communities before the water eventually drains into the Northwest Territories and the Arctic Ocean.

For Lenny Hansen, the Athabasca River has always been a part of his life, since he was a kid growing up in Fort McMurray. He's caught walleye, northern pike and other fish, with frequent sightings of other wildlife near the banks such as bears, moose and geese.
For 33 years, he worked in the oilsands. In retirement, he's a tour guide taking visitors up the river in his boat.
For him, treat-and-release is not a concern.
"I think it's a great idea and I've seen what they do. I think it's a really good process," said Hansen, a member of the Fort McMurray Métis District 17.
Alberta oilsands push for a decision on toxic tailings ponds
Frustrations growing
Treating and releasing tailings pond water into the Athabasca River has alarmed some Indigenous leaders and their communities.

When representatives from Suncor Energy visited Fort Chipewyan last month, they hoped to demonstrate to the community how their treatment technology worked. Instead, they quickly left when they were greeted by protesters.

Chief Melody Lepine leads the Mikisew Cree First Nation (MCFN), which is based in the Fort Chipewyan region, north of Fort McMurray. She feels the provincial government is forcing her community to accept treat-and-release, especially after the federal and provincial governments signed their MOU this past summer.

Lepine said the protest against Suncor came from a feeling among residents that their concerns are being ignored. She said her First Nation would consider legal action if her community felt treat-and-release threatened Fort Chipewyan.
"This is not the first time where things have been forced, in terms of decisions made that impact us, that we have to deal with the consequences later," she said.
"Exploring all of the options of how to reverse those decisions and activities would be definitely something we would seriously consider."

items: ‘Environmental racism’: Fort Chipewyan residents protest proposed treat-and-release plan for tailings water

blocks.text: At least one Indigenous-led company in the region hopes to find an alternative. Tũ Nipi Water Solutions was recently given conditional approval of a $4.6 million provincial grant to begin researching other proposals for treating tailings.

The company's CEO, Ron Quintal, hopes to find technology that can treat and reuse — not release — tailings water. He says the fear behind treat-and-release among Indigenous people is because of "generational trauma" associated with water.

There are fears that contamination from the oilsands has made its way into waterbodies and contributed to cancers in Fort Chipewyan, for instance. Lepine points to the 5.2 million litres of oilsands wastewater that overflowed from Imperial Oil's Kearl Lake facility in 2023.
"We don't drink the water in the community and that's going back to that generational trauma," said Quintal, who is also the former president of Fort McKay Métis Nation.
"Treat-and-release is not something that my ownership, my leadership and my community could ever support," he said, describing debate about the issue as "white hot."

items: Alberta separation group releases report touting affordable transition to independence
After 'doom and gloom' decade, Fort McMurray readies for a boom

blocks.text: Lepine also wants to see industry groups and different levels of government pursue alternatives to treat-and-release. She says the only way MCFN would accept treat-and-release is if leadership are confident the technology will not harm human health or the environment.
"But we're nowhere near that today," she said.
"It is a situation of environmental racism. We often say if the rivers flew in the opposite direction to non-Indigenous communities, would things be like this?"
Oilsands facilities are shown near the Athabasca River at Suncor's Base Plant near Fort McMurray. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)
Pressure on Ottawa to act
Industry players say they have spent several years developing and testing various technologies to treat the wastewater, in addition to supporting ongoing water monitoring programs in the region.

"If we take these elements together, we think that gives confidence that a treatment technology is effective, environmentally protective and capable of building, delivering long term results," said Jessica Dillabough, a sustainability manager with Imperial Oil.

The industry is testing various chemical and biological methods of treating tailings water and filtering out contaminants. Major oil companies have partnered with university scientists on dozens of research projects focused on water and tailings in the oilsands.

items: Banned for decades, releasing oilsands tailings water is now on the horizon

blocks.text: For now, Ottawa is tight-lipped about its next move. The federal environment minister declined interview requests from CBC News and a spokesperson wouldn't provide any timeline on a decision.

Last month, federal Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson answered a question from Radio-Canada during a press conference in Alberta about tailings ponds, remarking "We will do the work to make sure we have the right regulations with respect to tailings ponds."
Hodgson said the regulations would be developed by the end of 2027.
However, later that day, his spokesperson said to CBC News that the minister had misspoken and there is no timeline.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith attends the Oil Sands Expo in Fort McMurray on Sept. 16. The oilsands industry should be able to release treated water into the river, she said, similar to the regulations allowing other industries to do the same. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

articles.title: This Canadian-Punjabi rapper was murdered in 2022. His new tour is testing the market for holographic concerts
articles.summary: Sidhu Moose Wala’s Signed to God world tour kicked off in Toronto last Friday, with a hologram standing in on stage for the Canadian-Punjabi rap star who was shot and killed in 2022. Fans lined up…

image.caption: Canadian-Punjabi rapper Sidhu Moose Wala was shot to death in 2022 in northern India. Four years later, a hologram version of the late star opened his Signed to God hologram world tour in Toronto Friday, testing the technology's ability to deliver a memorable fan experience at a premium price. (Sidh

blocks.text: Business·New

Sidhu Moose Wala’s Signed to God world tour kicked off in Toronto last Friday, with a hologram standing in on stage for the Canadian-Punjabi rap star who was shot and killed in 2022. Fans lined up for the show seemed eager to see what was in store, while tech and music industry observers say it's an intersting test of the technology.
Some tickets advertised online for shows in Toronto and Vancouver cost $2,000 after taxes and fees

Ravinder Sidhu and his sister Nav travelled to Toronto from India to see Sidhu Moose Wala’s Signed to God world tour kick off at Scotiabank Arena last Friday, dropping $550 each on tickets. They knew it would be no ordinary performance.

That's because the Canadian-Punjabi rapper died in 2022 after gunmen fired a hail of bullets into a vehicle he was in near his hometown in Northern India. A hologram replaced Moose Wala on stage Friday, testing the technology’s ability to deliver a memorable fan experience at a premium price.
"Maybe it will be futuristic," Ravinder told CBC News outside the venue before the show. "We can't express it. We're over-excited."

items: Famous Punjabi-language rapper Sidhu Moose Wala shot dead in India
Why Sidhu Moose Wala's violent death has sent shock waves from Punjab to Brampton

blocks.text: Another fan, Harry Singh, says he spent $270 for his ticket, plus airfare from California.
"If you waited until last minute, that same ticket I got is now like $1,500," Singh told CBC News hours before the show. "I got pretty lucky. I bought them early."
How much would you spend on a hologram concert?
Some tickets for the Toronto show advertised online cost nearly $2,000 before taxes and fees. Prices for the next stop in Vancouver on Thursday are similar.
"They're saying it's going to look like it's completely real, but we'll find out," Singh said.

In a text message after the show, he says the concert featured an unreleased song called Rebirth, and an on-stage appearance by the late rapper's younger brother. In one video he recorded during the show, Singh is seen surrounded by a sea of smartphones held in the air as people sing along with the crowd and the hologram of Moose Wala on stage.

Sidhu Moose Wala, a Canadian-Punjabi rapper who was shot and killed in northern India in 2022, appeared on stage as a hologram during a concert on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026 at Toronto's Scotiabank Arena. (Submitted by Harry Singh)
From ABBA to Ozzy

Music journalist and historian Alan Cross says the rise of digital-first performances is real. He points to the commercial success of ABBA Voyage in London, which features de-aged digital avatars of the Swedish pop group performing with a live 10-piece band.

A cohort of aging rock stars, the transfer of musical catalogues into the hands of savvy investors, and modern audiences accustomed to the digital world are all things he says will contribute to the growing holographic concert trend.
"Not only do artists become stubbornly dead, but they also get tired. They want vacations. They want to spend time with their families," Cross told CBC News in an interview.
"In the next five years we're going to see a mass extinction event with all these rock and roll heroes and music heroes that we've known our entire lives," he said.
He noted that though their deaths are inevitable, technology can give them a second life on stage because "we're raising a new generation of people who live digitally."

items: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected — and the ethics are murky
Are holograms the real deal? Musicians confront questions of ethics, quality

blocks.text: David Nussbaum, founder of Los Angeles-based hologram company Proto says using the technology to bring back stars who have died "makes a lot of sense."
"We're working with Jack and Sharon Osborne right now to bring back Ozzy, who passed just about a year ago."

Nussbaum calls his company's recreation of the Black Sabbath frontman an "agentic AI avatar." Not only does it possess encyclopedic knowledge of Osbourne’s work and public life, he says it can speak to fans in languages the real rock star never knew.

"If you're Chinese and you ask that question in Chinese, he's gonna answer you in Chinese. If you're Italian, and you asked him that question in Italian, he's going to answer you in Italian," he said.
He says that with hundreds of dialects available, fans can communicate with their favourite artists, living or dead, in the language of their choice. "This is the ultimate form of connecting."
Once the stuff of fiction, people have been developing this technology for entertainment purposes for years.
Flash back to 14 years ago, when another famous rap star murdered in his prime was digitally resurrected for thousands of fans at the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival.

Rapper Snoop Dogg, left, and a hologram of the late rapper Tupac Shakur perform onstage during the third day of the 2012 Coachella Valley Music & Arts Festival at the Empire Polo Field in Indio, Calif. (Christopher Polk/Getty Images)
"I don't think I'm the only one who watched that video of Tupac Shakur at Coachella in 2012," said tech expert Carmi Levy.

"It almost felt like lightning had struck the entertainment and tech industries at the same time," said Levy, noting that the experience of viewing video hadn't changed much for generations until that Coachella set, which "used some very cutting-edge techniques for the time."
He also noted that the quality of the technology has improved a lot since 2012, and continues to evolve with advancements in artificial intelligence.
What's next?
Proto's Nussbaum agrees and says his company aims to "seamlessly integrate" realistic, AI-powered holograms into the real world.

Proto's products include a life-sized holographic display units that project photorealistic, 4K volumetric people or objects inside a light box, allowing subjects to beam in live, or interact with AI avatars.

"The olden days of hologram performances were mostly magic tricks and theater and fun experiences. But now, this technology, although it's being used quite a bit in music and entertainment, most of the time it's been used in enterprise," he told CBC News.

items: Holograms, headsets and health care: The future is now

blocks.text: "It's being used by doctors to beam into rural remote clinics, where patients are having trouble finding expert doctors and health care providers. It's being used by educators to beam onto lecture stages from all over the world, without having to get onto an airplane and fly to a college or university. It's been used in museums. It's being used in lots of different settings."
Nussbaum's company is also expanding the celebrity hologram experience off the stage.

He says Proto recently worked with Bon Jovi during the band’s residency at New York’s Madison Square Garden to create what it called an interactive hologram of rock star Jon Bon Jovi so fans could pose for realistic-looking photos.
Levy says it’s only a matter of time before consumers can enjoy holographic experiences at home.

items: Yukon First Nation uses holograms to preserve the knowledge of elders
How 3D holograms and AI are preserving Holocaust survivors' stories

blocks.text: "If you look at the typical smartphone today, which has photo and video capabilities that would have made an advanced photographer and videographer blush just a few years ago, it's easy to appreciate that at some point, advanced 3D AI capabilities — holographic capabilities even — will ultimately be built into the multimedia capabilities of a smartphone, or whatever it is that replaces it," he said.
"The industry is certainly heading toward that point."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse resurrects the classic vampire hunting game in bold, bloody fashion
articles.summary: Belmont's Curse is mostly a roaring resurrection for the 40-year-old series — but its punishing difficulty could make it hard to recommend to newcomers to the genre.

image.caption: Rose Belmont is the new main character in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, the latest in the long-running Castlevania series of video games. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

blocks.text: Entertainment·Review
Belmont's Curse is mostly a roaring resurrection for the 40-year-old series — but its punishing difficulty could make it hard to recommend to newcomers to the genre.
It's an old-school adventure with flair, but Nintendo Switch version suffers from technical flaws
With its monster-fighting action, punishing difficulty and boppy soundtrack, 1986's Castlevania was a standout title on the Nintendo Entertainment System.

In the nearly 40 years since, the series has spawned dozens of sequels, spinoffs and crossover media. But the publisher, Japan's Konami, has let it slumber like a vampire in a coffin; its last new instalment came out in 2014.

Now, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse aims to bring in new and old fans alike by taking inspiration from the wildly different chapters of the series' history as well as independent games it's inspired over the years.

The result is mostly a roaring resurrection for the series blending old-school 2D exploration with breathtaking artistic direction — but its punishing difficulty could make it hard to recommend to newcomers to the genre.
Back to the Belmonts
Belmont's Curse puts players in control of Rose Belmont, monster hunter and daughter of Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades, two of the main characters from 1989's Castlevania 3: Dracula's Curse.
It's 1499 and Paris is burning, under attack from monsters of unknown origin. Trevor shuffles offscreen to look for the local bishop, while Rose looks for clues in the Paris streets.
Dracula's castle rises from the ground, surrounded by Paris in 1499. (All screenshots were captured from a build still in development.) (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

She's also inherited a curse — a blood-red mark creeping up her right arm — from her mother who succumbed to it after a battle with Dracula over 20 years prior. Losing control of her emotions and giving into hate risks turning Rose into a mindless monster not unlike her enemies.

Things quickly go from bad to worse. Only a few hours into the adventure, Trevor is captured and Dracula's castle rises from underneath Paris, seemingly destroying Notre Dame Cathedral in the process.

Various members of the Belmont family tree have been the main characters of most Castlevania games, and centring it back on them makes sense — not the least because Trevor and Sypha recently starred in the Netflix Castlevania animated series. Through the game's roughly 15- to 20-hour runtime, however, the story will plumb both obvious and surprising corners of the series' decades-long history.
Dynamic combat and movement

Belmont's Curse roughly follows the same format as the fan-favourite 1997 entry Symphony of the Night. Taking cues from Nintendo's Metroid and Zelda series, Rose can explore Paris and Dracula's castle with its labyrinthine and interlocking locations, from an eerie cemetery where ghosts haunt visitors freely, or a clock tower full of giant metal gears and deadly machinery.
Rather than completing linear levels in sequence, players will run into dead ends or impassable hazards, eventually returning to them after discovering a new ability or equipment.
Dangerous traps and obstacles litter Paris and Dracula's castle. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

Early on, for example, Rose gets a whip that she can use to swing over spike traps or lasso enemies, opening them up for an exhilarating powerful attack with her weapons including swords, lances and yes, more whips.

The so-called "Metroidvania" formula is a proven one, and it feels like coming back home seeing it here after years of indie games imitating and iterating upon it — such as the mega-popular Hollow Knight: Silksong from last year.
Rose uses a whip made of magical light as a grappling hook. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)
It's hard. Maybe too hard?

Players should use caution, however — while familiar monster types rear their heads again such as zombies, skeletons and floating medusa heads, everyone moves faster and hits much harder than in past entries.

You'll have to use all your wits and reflexes to get Rose through some pitched battles, especially early on as her health and magic resources start small unless she finds upgrades hidden throughout the map.
Rose battles Medusa in an early boss fight. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

Even more punishing are the trap rooms — spinning razor blades, spiky pits and more arranged in devilish gauntlets that require timing just a little too precise, or jumping through gaps just a little too narrow to do reliably. Every new ability you find that theoretically makes them easier to navigate, only allows the level designers to add new ways to torment you.
Retracing your steps

This can make the need to backtrack and explore previously-seen areas all the more grating. Most older Castlevania games in this mold were fairly generous with rooms where you can save your progress and heal up, or warp rooms to zip back to relative safety.

Such sanctuaries are relatively rare in Belmont's Curse. Too often you'll need to backtrack for minutes at a time before reaching anything new, or even a place to breathe before planning your next route.
A section of the map in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, showing the interconnected parts of Paris the player must explore. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)
There are difficulty settings that, for example, let you adjust how much damage enemies' strikes inflict on Rose; but they don't ease the trap rooms' demands or make backtracking less tiresome.
Striking art and soundtrack
Despite the occasional frustrations navigating the maze that is Belmont's Curse, the package is elevated by exceptional presentation and art direction.

Paris is swathed in brilliant colour palettes from the pitch-black catacombs with flickering orange or eerie green flames puncturing the darkness; to the relatively serene cemetery's verdant greens and yellows getting gradually more poisonous as you delve deeper into its dangerous sewers.
Players can find items to upgrade their health and magic levels in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)

Perhaps the height of it is the first approach to Dracula's castle, an impossibly huge and baroque structure set atop the ruins of Paris, supporting chain links the size of buildings anchoring it to the ground, as Rose whips and slashes her way through stone gargoyles haunted suits of armour — all set to a booming remix of the series classic song Bloody Tears.

Special mention goes to the soundtrack in general, a mostly brand-new group of tracks effortlessly mixing the series' usual classical foundation of choral chants and organ pipes with lo-fi beats and even the occasional dubstep reverberations.
A giant skull looms over Rose in the catacombs below Paris. (Motion Twin & Evil Empire/Konami)
The story is also anchored by surprisingly poignant performances by voice actors, particularly Abby Trott as Rose and JB Blanc as a remorseful creature initially known only as The Fallen.
Switch version seriously falters

A word of caution, however: the Nintendo Switch version suffered from serious performance flaws in the review period as it was released on the original hardware and not the newer Switch 2 (though it can be played on either).

We experienced grainy, low-res visuals and longer load times on that platform, but worst was significant input delay between pressing a button and Rose moving or jumping on the screen. In a game that requires near-instant reaction times, this made the experience nearly unplayable.

The visuals and responsiveness were much better on the Xbox Series X version we played to completion. Konami says a Day 1 update will improve these issues on all platforms, but it wasn't available by the time this review was filed.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jonathan Ore is a writer and editor for CBC Radio Digital in Toronto. He regularly covers the video games industry for CBC Radio programs across the country and has also covered arts & entertainment, technology and the games industry for CBC News. You can reach him at jonathan.ore@cbc.ca

articles.title: Pope Leo in Rome hospital for lung surgery
articles.summary: Leo has been unusually candid for a pontiff about his health issues, disclosing the surgery to thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.

image.caption: The surgery marks the first major health issue of Leo's 17-month papacyImage: Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV is to undergo surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung, the Vatican has confirmed, and determine if it is cancerous.
He is being seen at Rome's prestigious Gemelli hospital, which has been the main site of treatment for popes for decades.
Shift in transparency
Leo, 71, disclosed the issue to thousands of worshippers at a prayer service on Sunday, making a marked shift in the level of transparency about his health compared to his predecessors.
In the past, the Vatican has often been accused of making confusing or extremely vague statements about popes' health, if revealing at information at all.
Pope Leo to undergo lung nodule surgery

The pontiff will be put under general anesthesia and require a weeklong hospital stay. All of his engagements have been cancelled through October 20. He is still likely to take a planned trip to South America in November.
According to oncologists, this type of surgery is usually necessary to determine if a lump is malignant. However, if it is, Leo has an excellent prognosis since it was caught so early.

articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Second Division on Tuesday acquitted Iloilo Rep. Janette Garin and her co-accused of graft charges in connection with the alleged unlawful procurement of P3.5 billion worth of…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 3:39pm Updated October 13, 2026 3:45pm

The Sandiganbayan Second Division on Tuesday acquitted Iloilo Rep. Janette Garin and her co-accused of graft charges in connection with the alleged unlawful procurement of P3.5 billion worth of Dengvaxia vaccines in 2015.
Among her co-accused were former Health undersecretaries Gerardo Bayugo and Kenneth Hartigan-Go, as well as former officials of the Philippine Children's Medical Center (PCMC).
The charges stemmed from the Aquino administration's procurement of the anti-dengue vaccines for a school-based immunization program.
In a statement, Garin welcomed the Sandiganbayan's decision, saying the acquittal vindicated the work of scientists and public health experts who supported the dengue vaccination program.
“Natutuwa kami (We're happy about it). This is a win not for me but for our scientists and experts,” Garin said following the release of the Sandiganbayan's decision.

“Our researchers, scientists and public health experts continued to attend the hearings in this case. We understand that there are anti-vaccine advocates, but we cannot neglect our duties or the vaccination effort because vaccination saves lives,” she added.
Garin also urged the public not to “demonize” vaccines, saying she would leave it to experts to address dengue immunization in the country.

Prosecutors alleged that Garin and four other officials conspired to unlawfully realign government funds for the purchase of Dengvaxia, which had not yet been included in the Department of Health's (DOH) Expanded Program on Immunization or listed in the Philippine National Drug Formulary.
The Office of the Ombudsman filed graft and technical malversation charges against the officials before the Sandiganbayan in October 2023 over alleged irregularities in the procurement.

Garin earlier denied allegations that funds had been illegally diverted to purchase the vaccines, maintaining that the allocation had been approved by the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and covered by a Special Allotment Release Order (SARO).
Meanwhile, Hartigan-Go previously denied promoting Dengvaxia despite having worked for a foundation linked to the vaccine's distributor.
“We never promoted any product, advertised or sold through the foundation,” said Hartigan-Go, who served as executive director of the Zuellig Family Foundation from 2001 to 2009.

The Dengvaxia controversy erupted in 2017 after French pharmaceutical company Sanofi Pasteur disclosed that the vaccine could increase the risk of severe dengue among individuals who had not previously been infected with the virus.
The government subsequently suspended the dengue immunization program, which had already covered hundreds of thousands of schoolchildren.— with reports from Llanesca Panti/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Fact check: Marcos video taken out of context to claim 2028 elections will be scrapped
articles.summary: An edited Marcos video falsely claims he plans to stop the 2028 elections.

blocks.text: October 13, 2026 | 3:37pm
President Bongbong Marcos at the Kapihan with the Media in Singapore on Oct. 11, 2026.
RTVM / Screenshot
MANILA, Philippines — An edited video of President Bongbong Marcos circulating on social media falsely claims he plans to change the Constitution to prevent the 2028 elections.
Facebook and TikTok posts shared edited footage of President Bongbong Marcos with text overlays falsely claiming he plans to prevent the 2028 elections.
Screenshot taken Oct. 13, 2026, 12 p.m
Two Facebook reels posted on October 12 used spliced footage of Marcos with text overlays claiming he intended to stop the upcoming presidential elections.
The overlays read, “BBM babaguhin ang Constitution para walang election sa 2028” and “No election in 2028 is the main goal."
A similar claim appeared in a TikTok post on the same date, using the same spliced footage with similar text overlays.
The TikTok post’s caption read:
BBM NADULAS ANG BIBIG. WALANG PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION SA 2028 AT BABAGOHIN ANG CONSTITUTION. #news #balita #breakingnews
Rating: This is false.
Facts
The circulating videos used footage from Marcos’ October 11 clarification of his “buwaon” remark.

In the full exchange, Marcos said his reaction referred to a report about changing the Constitution in relation to the elections, not an announcement that he planned to prevent the 2028 presidential elections.

While in Singapore, Marcos said his “buwaon” statement to Palace Press Officer Claire Castro was not meant to be an official press release and was not specifically directed at Vice President Sara Duterte.
"Ba’t mo sinabi sa kanila ‘yun? That was only supposed to be between the two of us. That was – my reaction was to changing the Constitution to the elections,” he said.

On September 28, Castro relayed Marcos’ reaction to Duterte’s allegations that the administration was seeking to bring her down. Duterte made the statement while denying claims by Police Corporal Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered more than P2 billion in cash to the vice president.
In a September 26 Facebook statement, Duterte called this "another media stunt" and an "attempt to breathe life into a faltering impeachment case."
“The desperation of the administration to bring me down, push for Charter Change, prevent the 2028 elections, and cling to power is becoming increasingly diabolical,” she said.
In response, Malacañang called Duterte’s allegations "nonsense" and “fake news.”
"Ito po mismo ay mensahe ng Pangulo patungkol sa komento na iyan ng Bise Presidente, ang sabi po niya, 'Iyan po ay non-sense, fake news, mahilig magsinungaling, mga buwaon,'" Castro said.
Why we fact-checked this
Multiple posts carrying similar claims have gained traction on social media as the 2028 elections draw near and the impeachment trial against the vice president is ongoing.

As of October 13, the Facebook reels have gained at least 58,000 views, 800 reactions, 300 comments and 300 shares each. Meanwhile, the TikTok video has obtained more than 36,000 views, 600 likes, and 150 comments. — with reports from Martin Ramos

articles.title: Alan Peter Cayetano: Impeachment trial has no time limit
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano on Tuesday raised concerns regarding timeline following the decision of the prosecution to drop three out of the four Articles of Impeachment against Vice…

blocks.text: Published October 13, 2026 3:25pm

Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano on Tuesday raised concerns regarding timeline following the decision of the prosecution to drop three out of the four Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte, saying that the proceedings should not be hastened for the sake of fairness.
On Day 39 of the trial, Cayetano stressed that there is no limit in the Constitution when it comes to the conduct of the impeachment trial.

“We can finish this in January, we can finish this in February. We can take a break tomorrow and focus on the budget. It is our choice. Kung ako masusunod, unahin natin ang budget--may super El Niño, hindi pa tapos ang flood control investigation,” he said.
(If it were up to me, we should prioritize the budget first—there is a super El Niño, and the flood control investigation isn't finished yet.)
“It’s in the best interest of everyone that there’s fairness and we take our time. There’s no time limit. Who is saying that we have to finish this by November?"
Cayetano said he himself wants the trial to be finished, but not at the expense of deliberating on and passing the proposed 2027 national budget.

"I want it finished. But between finishing it tapos may unfairness, and finishing it na unahin ‘to kesa sa budget---Mr. Presiding Officer, Mr. Senate President, you know I’d like to put on record, I’m very uncomfortable with that. I think it will be a disservice to the Filipino people,” he added.
The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday accepted the move by the House prosecution panel to withdraw three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Vice President Sara Duterte.
The charges dropped were Articles I, III and IV, which detail allegations of misuse of confidential funds, bribery, and grave threats, respectively.
The minority leader said that the impeachment proceedings must be finished “with the basic element of fairness [and] justice.”
“Kahit anong mangyari dito---acquit or convict---may matutuwa, may magagalit. But history will judge us whether or not ‘yung elementary fairness and due process,” Cayetano said.

(Whatever happens here---acquit or convict---some will be happy, some will be angry. But history will judge us as to whether or not we applied the elementary fairness and due process.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: The return of the prodigal son? Why speculation is rising over Josh Frydenberg’s future
articles.summary:
The spectre of a leadership alternative is hardly helpful for Angus Taylor. But would Frydenberg do a better job?

  • Get our

blocks.text: A reasonable query for Liberals at this point is: if Josh Frydenberg is the answer, what is the question?

There was a whiff of weariness in some corners of parliament this week, as the former treasurer and deputy Liberal leader happily stoked another round of “Josh for Canberra” speculation. With more rumoured comebacks than Oasis, Frydenberg’s latest foray into the national political arena saw him bouncing around TV, radio and podcast interviews to promote his new book, and pointedly refuse to rule out trying to rejoin the parliament.

His book – part family history, part treatise on antisemitism and social cohesion, part political manifesto – is titled A Grateful Son. But is he instead the prodigal son? The one who set out on his own but is destined to be welcomed back to the Liberal party family with joy and celebrations?

Frydenberg is young enough, bright enough and certainly energetic enough to still make a difference in public life. His addition to what is often a tired Coalition partyroom would certainly spice things up, and give a new weapon in their arsenal. The ideas in his book – a remix of the GST to fund income tax cuts, concerns about the future of his party, changes to the system of federalism, yet more calls for civic service for school leavers – are politically inconvenient for the federal Coalition as well as the Victorian Liberals headed for an election win, but are worth considering.

The talk around parliament is that Frydenberg is privately telling people he is unlikely to seek a return. But the fact he has pointedly refused to rule it out in a conga line of media interviews, saying only that he would make his mind up later, seems opportunistic. The spectre of a potential leadership alternative is hardly a help for Angus Taylor.

Labor sources have helpfully shared key quotes from Frydenberg’s book and media tour, pointing out his calls for changes to GST, the labour market, and criticisms of the Liberal trajectory – again, none helpful to the leader.

The problems facing the modern Liberal party, under Taylor’s leadership, are myriad. Its hostile right flank is barracking for Pauline Hanson and One Nation, its centre is still eyeing the teal independents, and Taylor – now eight months into the job – has a lower primary vote than when Sussan Ley was dumped. The Guardian Essential poll found the Coalition primary at a record low 22% in September, compared to 25% in January, a fortnight before Taylor rolled Ley.

These are all reasons for alarm for the centre right. It’s just not clear if Frydenberg is the answer to any of these problems. One question echoing around parliament this week was: would he do a better job than Taylor on anything substantive? In other words, is he yesterday’s man?

A return to the partyroom would give the Coalition a well-known face and a policy brain in a team which could benefit from both. Maybe Frydenberg would be content to return as a loyal soldier under Taylor, serving in an appropriately senior cabinet role. But maybe not. Few think he’d give up a well-paid job in banking to sit on the frontbench instead of the leader’s chair.

The loudest cheer Hanson got at last weekend’s Cpac conference was when she sledged Taylor, saying Australians didn’t want a “smarmy management consultant” replacing Anthony Albanese as prime minister. Would any of those voters more prefer the chairman of investment bank Goldman Sachs, the role Frydenberg currently holds? Taylor in recent times has tried throwing a bone to that fringe of the right-wing movement, producing more off-the-cuff videos with unpolished deliveries (and swearing) a la Hanson – would Frydenberg, at home in boardrooms and business lunches, be able to win back the voters furious at “politics as usual” and career politicians?

Maybe, then, Frydenberg could chart a course back to the middle for the Coalition: not chasing its right flank further to the fringe, but setting a mainstream course back toward the centre, where elections in Australia are won.

That would be a decent idea, if you forget how Frydenberg was ejected from parliament in the first place: bundled out in 2022 by Monique Ryan in the big community independents wave which swept half a dozen moderate-ish urban Liberals from their seats.

Ryan was supported by Climate 200. That group’s origin story may be relevant here: Simon Holmes à Court, a former donor to Frydenberg’s Kooyong 200 fundraising vehicle, was reportedly ejected from a supporter event and set up his own group in response. Climate 200 would hardly respond to Frydenberg’s comeback, or potential leadership, with party poppers and a “welcome back” card.

The teal wave which swept Frydenberg and several other moderate Liberals from office in 2022 hasn’t exactly swelled into a tsunami since then, and some could argue the conditions of four years ago are not there today – just ask Tim Wilson, who lost Goldstein to teal Zoe Daniel in 2022 but wrestled it back in 2025.
after newsletter promotion
No Liberals we spoke to this week were jazzed about the prospect of Frydenberg’s return, or the distraction it provides.
But if there were any people happy about his potential return, they were on the government benches.
Albanese joked to Labor’s caucus meeting today that Frydenberg was now the “shadow opposition leader”, claiming “Josh Frydenberg’s priority has always been Josh Frydenberg”.
“I’m surprised Josh Frydenberg isn’t trying to bump me off this program,” the PM joked on the ABC on Tuesday.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers claimed his old sparring partner was “stalking” Taylor for the leadership, proclaiming. One senior Labor source cheekily joked that we should call it “the Fryre Festival”, a reference to the ill-fated and chaotic Fyre Festival in 2017, which had its own short-lived and catastrophic comeback in 2024.
Frydenberg’s media tour is likely to continue over coming days. The speculation over his potential comeback will linger even longer – Labor will make sure of it.
