articles.title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
articles.summary: The actor, who played the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series, dies aged 34.

blocks.text: US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34.
"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC.
He died in Brownsville, Texas. No immediate cause of death was provided.

Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award in 2014 for his work on the series.
"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative Sean Reilly said in a statement to the BBC.
Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's.

He created The Mitte Foundation as well, to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said.
Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008 to 2013.

The anti-hero drama created by Vince Gilligan earned a whopping 58 Primetime Emmy nominations and won 16, including two for Outstanding Drama Series in 2013 and 2014. It is widely credited as being one of the best US TV series of the 21st century.

Cranston plays a high school chemistry teacher in New Mexico who turns to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis. As he descends deeper into the underbelly of the meth trade, he drifts further from his son, Walt Jr, who made his displeasure known with levity through much of the series.

articles.title: Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has had a whirlwind weekend, announcing a diesel deal with Russia and an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. With the midterms coming up, it looks like Trump is…

blocks.text: With elections that will decide control of Congress just weeks away and American voters already casting ballots in some battlegrounds, President Donald Trump has turned his eyes overseas – and to Russia, in particular - for help tackling one of his most pressing problems.
World affairs seldom provide easy answers, however, and developments elsewhere have threatened to undermine his efforts to bring down fuel prices before they provide any political benefit.

A whirlwind weekend started on Friday afternoon, as Trump announced a new deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide the US with hundreds of millions of tons of Russian diesel fuel in the coming months.

High energy prices, particularly for midwestern agricultural states that rely on diesel to power farm machinery and carry their goods to market, have been a growing source of frustration for American voters.

Polls suggest they view the Iran War as the leading cause for their woes, and overall support for Trump, and approval of his handling of the war and the US economy in particular, has dropped precipitously.

Trump heralded his Russian deal in a Truth Social post as bringing "lower prices for Americans," while he ordered his Treasury Department to suspend US restrictions that prevented Russian diesel from being sold on global markets.
Two days later, Trump was back on his social media website, touting a new energy ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine.
The truth, however, was more complicated.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had no advanced notice of the agreement, although he said his nation would abide by it. Russia, for its part, was silent. And on Sunday night, it launched a new wave of attacks on Ukrainian power plants.
"It's clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelensky noted wryly on Monday. He added: "This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."

It now appears Trump's celebration of the "energy truce" may have been a familiar move for this president, touting an agreement before it had been sealed and delivered. In the past, for instance, he has prematurely announced Middle East ceasefires and sweeping peace agreements.

Whether it is impatience on the president's part with the slow pace of diplomacy or a savvy negotiating tactic to push a deal across the finish line, the result has been to set off a scramble as the world decides what it means – and how to react.
Those reactions didn't take long to arrive.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has become a vocal critic of the president's on the international stage, offered "strong support" for the energy ceasefire, but condemned the diesel deal as undermining peace and stability in Europe and helping Russia to finance its "illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine".

In the US, Trump's diesel announcement prompted similar concern, even among members of his own party. Four Republican senators joined with Democrats in a letter calling on the president to "immediately reverse course".

"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the senators wrote in a statement released on Sunday. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the US runs directly counter to that law."

What could be worse for the president than the criticisms is that the announced ceasefire has had little effect on the price of diesel, which continues to sit below its record highs but still well above $6 a gallon.
Meanwhile, as the latest twists in the Russia-Ukraine conflict unfolded, new violence in the Middle East threaten to further strain global energy markets, regardless of what happens with Russian oil.

A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on airports and energy infrastructure that killed at least 13 over the weekend, have threatened to escalate a decade-long conflict that had been simmering throughout the US-Iran war.

"This is the Houthis sending a message that it's not just military targets, it's not just energy infrastructure, they're going to strike at civilian airports that could kill a lot of people," Michael Ratney, former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told the BBC.

The US-Iran war was a conflict that none of the Arab nations in the region wanted, he said, and the latest Houthi offensive was a foreseeable result. With the US and Iran currently in an extended stand-off, any new hostilities could lead to more regional conflict and send oil prices soaring once more.
"I do think it gets uglier before it really deescalates," he said.

In recent weeks, Trump has pointed to Ukraine, not the Middle East, as the primary source of the world's energy woes. He cites increased oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which had been effectively shut by Iran's military threat.
That may, however, be wishful thinking – an attempt to convince the American public to direct their energy-related anger toward a conflict that began under a different president's watch.
There is only one president at a time, however. And when American voters casts their ballots they tend to hold those who are currently in power responsible.
After a rough weekend that again proved there are no easy fixes to the global energy crisis, that may be the worst news of all for the US president.

articles.title: Qantas flight grounded after bedbug outbreak
articles.summary: The flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled after passengers on the plane's previous journey complained of bug bites.

blocks.text: A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled on Saturday, after an outbreak of bedbugs on the plane.
During the previous flight on Friday - a nearly 17-hour journey from Perth to Rome - some passengers had complained that they were being bitten by bugs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.
They were reportedly given antihistamines to help ease the itch of the bites, but supplies ran out.
The Boeing 787 Dreamliner had to be grounded for "a deep clean", a Qantas spokesperson told the BBC.

"We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats," the spokesperson said.
All affected customers were provided with accommodation and were rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, the carrier said.

Bedbugs are small, wingless parasites that can live on clothes, furniture and bedding. Their bites can be itchy but they do not usually cause more serious health problems, the NHS website says, external.

But they can be difficult and expensive to get rid of. Treatment includes washing all bedding, clothing, and household materials like curtains on a hot wash and tumble dry, or they can be put in plastic bags in a freezer for three or four days.
Bedbugs causing travel chaos is not unusual - less than two weeks ago, several Southeastern train services in England were cancelled after drivers discovered the creepy-crawlies in their cabs.
In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family travelling from Vancouver to London, after they were left covered in bug bites from an overnight flight.

And Turkish Airlines faced with a PR nightmare last year after the New York Times reported, external of several instances of bedbug infestations on its planes - and allegations at the time that the airline did nothing about it.

articles.title: Prominent U.S. archbishop compares planned livestream of firing squad execution to terrorist practices
articles.summary: Catholics serving in the U.S. army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood ‌shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S.…

image.caption: U.S. Military Services Archbishop Timothy Broglio, seen here in 2025, has raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to ​broadcast the execution of a former U.S. army officer who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. (Stephanie Scarbrough/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Catholics serving in the U.S. army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood ‌shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S. archbishop said on Monday.
Timothy Broglio urged Catholic members assigned to the firing squad to request religious exemption

In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the U.S. armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to ​broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort ​Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.

Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan's victims, and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the U.S. ​wanted to "imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically ⁠killing our adversaries."
"I oblige any Catholics ⁠assigned to the firing squad to request to be ‌excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church," Broglio said.
U.S. army regulations do allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations, and the army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad.
The Pentagon says Nidal Hasan will be executed by firing squad in a livestreamed broadcast in December. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Handout/Reuters)
Backlash from Republicans, international observers

U.S. War Secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth announced plans to livestream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and international observers. U.S. President Donald Trump approved Hasan's execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the ‌livestreaming to proceed.

The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the U.S. military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been ​shot by police during his arrest.

items: Vance, Republican lawmakers and religious leaders oppose Pentagon plan to livestream an execution
The U.S. plans to livestream an execution. Here's how that compares to global practice

blocks.text: Hegseth said last week he wants U.S. soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and ⁠location of Hasan's shooting spree. Hegseth has argued that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent.

Broglio ⁠questioned whether the effect of a livestreamed execution on young viewers had been considered. He said the U.S. military ⁠had ⁠a good reputation and asked if there ​was "really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of ​a man in a wheelchair to ⁠the whole world."

Broglio's statement was issued shortly after he met on Monday in Rome with Pope Leo, who has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war. Leo on Saturday condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically.
U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get livestreamed, he would ⁠not watch it.

articles.title: Windsor residents react to thank you banner from Detroit on Thanksgiving
articles.summary: A banner was flown above the Detroit River on Monday to thank Canadians during Thanksgiving. The initiative was organized by groups in Detroit, who wanted to commemorate the unique relationship…

blocks.text: Windsor

A banner was flown above the Detroit River on Monday to thank Canadians during Thanksgiving. The initiative was organized by groups in Detroit, who wanted to commemorate the unique relationship between Windsor and the American city.
The initiative was organized by groups from the U.S. side of the Detroit River
Here's why this Thanksgiving banner flew over the Detroit River
Windsor residents are reacting to a thank you banner that was flown over the Detroit River on Monday.
The nine-by-three-metre aerial banner, which reads "Detroit and Canada are bridged in friendship,” was organized by the Downtown Detroit Partnership (DDP) and Metro Detroit.
Eric Larson, CEO of the DDP, said the gesture is about reminding Windsorites of the importance of U.S.-Canada friendship at a time of cross-border friction.

"What better time than on Canada's Thanksgiving to recognize and really send an expression of gratitude," Larson said. "On the U.S. side, we find ourselves saying sorry a lot more than what used to be the custom."
Windsor residents are being impacted by tariffs on Canada's automotive sector, with Stellantis saying they contributed to recent layoffs.

items: Stellantis says tariffs, consumer demand driving weeks-long layoffs at Windsor plant

blocks.text: In July, tensions, tariffs and delays over the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge meant that only Canadian officials attended the official ribbon-cutting ceremony.
Larson said that Monday's banner event is a small gesture in recognizing Canada's importance.
"It's just the ability to recognize Canada's continued consistent leadership," he said.
Not crossing the border
The banner was flown along the Detroit River both morning and afternoon, and was visible to residents on both sides of the border.
Windsorites expressed gratitude at the gesture but acknowledged that they are unwilling to cross into the United States as trade tensions continue.

items: Windsor businesses looking for tariff help are still waiting

blocks.text: Windsor resident Jack Paterson said tensions with the Trump administration have meant that he has avoided crossing over into Detroit.
"The Americans are not our problem, it's the president and the Republican Party in power," Paterson said. " They stirred it up, divided everywhere and it's unsettling."
The banner was flown above the Detroit River for Canadian Thanksgiving. (Justin Escoto/CBC)
Despite the tensions, Paterson said he thinks that the banner reinforces the strength of Windsor and Detroit's unique relationship.
"I'm really moved by it just because we're not enemies of any kind with the American people," he said. "We enjoyed for years going over. We have relatives. It's all connected. We're all connected."
Local resident Priscilla Boismier came to the Detroit River to see the banner. (Justin Escoto/CBC)
Similarly, Priscilla Boismier said that while the aerial banner is a positive gesture, she is still hesitant to visit the American side of the river any time soon.
"It's a nice gesture considering what we're going through," Boismier said. "I don't have a passport. I don't intend to get a passport until Donald Trump is out of office."
For another local, Wayne Jahn, the banner is symbolic of Detroit's attachment to its neighbour.
"Michiganers love Canadians and vice versa," Jahn said. "We love them. But the situation dictates our reactions, and it's just too bad it's that way."
Once a regular visitor, Wayne Jahn says he hasn't crossed into the U.S. for two years. (Justin Escoto/CBC)
For Eric Larson, the banner is just a small way in which residents on both sides of the border can be reminded of their interconnectivity.
"We hope and expect this to be a moment in time and we can, you know, return to what has been a very successful, both economically and socially, relationship," he said.
"It's about how North America operates as one ecosystem."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Oliver Thompson is a writer, producer and musician. Originally from the UK, where he worked for the BBC, Oliver moved to Canada in 2018.
With files from Justin Escoto

articles.title: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
articles.summary: While Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggests he would sign up to a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, Russia has said little.

blocks.text: On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly.
So who is saying what?
Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed.
Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up – if Russia does.
Russia is saying: Very little.
Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists.
"Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied.
"As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you."
Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has.
It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow.
"Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded.
"It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery.
"That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway.
"But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have.
"In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it."
In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's.
In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country.
Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests – as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November.
Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel.
Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices.
Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv.
Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv.
It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine.
Moscow's reaction?
"The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said.
"Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that.
On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections.
That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer.
It comes as no surprise though.
Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting.

Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting.
On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning.
"This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written.
The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation.
Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal.

articles.title: UK: Iran 'highly likely' to be behind RAF Fairford incident
articles.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham told parliament there were "strong indications" of Iranian involvement. The government summoned Iran's ambassador. The scare at RAF Fairford led to the withdrawal of USAF…

image.caption: PM Andy Burnham said it would 'almost certainly' be Iran's IRGC that was pulling the stringsImage: House of Commons/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: The British government has accused Iran of involvement in a security alert outside a UK/US airbase in southern England last month, summoning the ambassador and announcing sanctions against two individuals.

Five British nationals were arrested in the vicinity of the RAF Fairford airbase on September 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses. They were later released on bail under strict conditions, and another arrest followed days later.

Police had already said they were considering the possibility of a foreign state actor's involvement, not least given RAF Fairford's importance to the US Air Force as one of the European bases that handles heavy bombers like B-1's and B-52's, with ample range to reach Iran.

blocks.caption: Some of the more advanced US bombers at RAF Fairford were ordered home after the incident [FILE: September 29, 2026]Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did Prime Minister Andy Burnham tell parliament?
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in the House of Commons on Monday that the UK might yet put further sanctions on Iran in response.
He said there were indications of Iran coordinating the potential plot.

"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," he said. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil."
The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited.

Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the vans. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum.

"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said.

blocks.caption: Burnham told the Commons that Iran could potentially face further sanctionsImage: House of Commons/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Foreign Secretary Miliband says Iranian ambassador summoned
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil."

Iran's state news agency IRNA reported Ambassador Ali Moussavi as "categorically rejecting the accusations" and calling on the British government "to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
Miliband said that two individuals would be subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification.
He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network.

Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas."

blocks.caption: How viable or dangerous the attack plot really was remains something of an open question, what's certain is that the young men were able to cause a major disturbance and an international incident [FILE: September 27, 2026]Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Joint statement from 29 countries condemns 'Iran's use of violent attacks'
Shortly afterwards, a total of 29 countries issued a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks."
It said these included "the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."

All of the so-called "Five Eyes" alliance and most European NATO members were listed among the signatories, including but not limited to the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Spain and Ireland.
In the aftermath of the September 27 incident at Fairford, the high-tech US B-1 bombers left the airbase. The older and larger contingent of B-52's remained there.
RAF Fairford is one of several airbases in southern England with a large US usage footprint. It's located around two hours' drive west of London, in a rural area north of Swindon.

As with most such bases, it can trace its roots back to the second World War when Nazi Germany occupied most of mainland Europe and Allied powers were operating air raids and preparing for the D-Day landings out of Britain.

articles.title: Slow down a honey bee stinging and you see impressive mechanisms at work
articles.summary: New research is showing what makes honeybee stings an effective, self-driving weapon. High speed cameras reveal how the stinger uses a double-piston that pumps up and down to drive it deeper while…

image.caption: High speed videography of an experiment captures how a western honey bee's stinger embeds itself deeper. (Ramirez Esquivel et al. 2026)

blocks.text: Science

New research is showing what makes honeybee stings an effective, self-driving weapon. High speed cameras reveal how the stinger uses a double-piston that pumps up and down to drive it deeper while delivering its poison.
New research slows down and shines light on a fatal defense mechanism
The stinger of a western honey bee (Apis mellifera) is a weapon of last resort, designed to embed itself and deposit venom in flesh — most often resulting in the worker bee's death.
New research published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences is quite literally shedding light on what makes this defence mechanism so effective.

"Being able to actually film them in action was a brand new thing that is only really possible thanks to modern cameras," said Fiorella Ramirez Esquivel, lead author and postdoctoral researcher with Macquarie University in Australia.
A western honey bee's stinger in action

Because bee stings happen in the blink of an eye, Ramirez Esquivel and her team used cameras capable of capturing hundreds of frames per second. The translucence of the venom sac and stinger allowed them to use strong lighting to better outline the distinct structures inside.

The experiments used live honey bees, removing their stinger and killing them immediately after. Because the stinger remains active for only about two minutes once separated from the bee's body, Ramirez Esquivel said she had to work fast.

"I'm removing the stinger from the bee and then I have to stick it into this artificial [skin substitute] and I have about four millimetres of space where I have to get it exactly right," she told CBC News from Sydney.

At 100 frames per second, you can see two distinct pieces in the middle chamber between the long needle and the giant venom sac. These are valves that move past each other in a unique dance. (Ramirez Esquivel et al. 2026)
Double-piston design
The results show how two specialized valves are doing two jobs at once: driving the barbed stinger deeper while continuously pumping venom from the sac down into the flesh.
The paper describes it as a "double piston design," but the system is a lot more complex than a standard car engine, where a single piston moves up and down inside a cylinder.

"Now imagine that you have two of them, and they have to be moving past each other when they go past," Ramirez Esquivel said, "and as they reverse direction, they have to collapse so that the fluid can flow around it."

It's a delicate dance that the researchers recreated using 3D printing to better understand how the valves move past each other — allowing venom to keep flowing while also propelling the stinger deeper.

Juliana Rangel, professor of apiculture at Texas A&M University who was not involved in the study, said she found the videos fascinating because they go beyond the scanning electron microscope images and diagrams she's used to seeing.

"We have known forever [about the stinger and its parts] because we have been the victims of these stinging events for tens of thousands of years," Rangel said. "But we just didn't know, really, how that venom continues to be pumped for so long after the release of the stinging apparatus."
The study says twitches and minute movements of the stinger can continue for as long as 15 minutes.
Honey bees are a social species and experts say stinging has to punch above a singular purpose. (Joel Saget/AFP/Getty Images)
Kill and be killed

Leaving behind part of the body as a defence mechanism is called autotomy, but not all bees do it. The western honey bee is a social species whose colony functions as a "superorganism" that workers help protect. Its drastic defence mechanism has to punch above a small bee's weight.

"This stinging structure and the evolution of the stinging apparatus … it's kind of an insurance policy," Rangel told CBC News from College Station, Texas. "That the life was lost for a good cause, which is defence of the larger colony."

Rangel added that almost all other bees that sting don't have barbs that help the stinger remain embedded in an animal because, unlike female worker honey bees, they need to survive in order to reproduce. Female worker honey bees are sterile and don't produce offspring themselves.
Honey bee stingers also release pheromones, chemical signals that recruit other bees to join an attack against a threat.
The defence mechanism doesn't always work against tougher skin or fur, Rangel says, but barbs and continuous penetration likely improve the chances of warding off an attacker.
A page describing the stinger from The Anatomy of the Honey Bee by Robert E. Snodgrass, published in 1910. (Cornell University Library/The Internet Archive)
Nature as inspiration
Though native to Europe, western honey bees are now found around the world and have been studied for hundreds of years. Our relationship with them stretches even further.

"It goes back about 9,000 years," said Lauren Ponisio, associate professor and ecologist at the University of Oregon. "There are cave paintings that describe people actually harvesting honey and wax from colonies. It doesn't show up until the Egyptians that we start seeing active management."

Fast-forward to 1758, when Swedish biologist Carl Linnaeus scientifically classified the species. Their stingers, the study notes, were described in great detail in the early 1900s by American entomologist Robert E. Snodgrass.
But by using high-speed videography, researchers are revealing more about this complex system — findings that could potentially have medical applications.

"It's not stopping and starting like a … syringe. The plunger for a syringe, it goes down once and that's it," Ramirez Esquivel said. "But because we have two plungers effectively, then you can have continuous flow."
A black stingless bee (Trigona spinipes) is pictured at the Metropolitan Natural Park, a protected area in Panama City on January 26, 2025. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty)
Ponisio says this study also makes her wonder about other bees that produce honey but differ significantly from western honey bees, including species native to the Americas.
"It does lead to really interesting questions of … well, you have these other honey producing bees, why don't they have stingers? And how did that work out for them?" Ponisio said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Anand Ram is a reporter and producer with CBC's science and climate unit. He's worked as a reporter covering technology, business and the environment and as a producer with The National.

articles.title: Hundreds of French supermarkets hit by a cyberattack that defrosted refrigeration systems
articles.summary: Hundreds of French supermarkets saw their refrigeration systems defrosted, spoiling tons of frozen food. The unprecedented attack has raised serious questions about food security across Europe.

image.caption: Hackers targeted refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets overnight, spoiling tons of foodImage: Fred Tanneau/AFP

blocks.text: Hundreds of French supermarkets were forced to throw away perishable goods on Monday after hackers commandeered refrigeration systems across the country, spoiling stock at major chains in a sophisticated overnight cyberattack.

Hackers destroyed the food by taking control of refrigeration systems at Cooperative U, Leclerc, Les Mousquetaires, and Intermarche stores across the country and then defrosting thousands of freezer and refrigeration units.
During the overnight attack, in some cases, fully-stocked fridges were heated up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for more than six hours.
Over 400 stores were hit according to retailers.
Prosecutors in Paris confirmed the attacks and said fires had been reported at some locations.
Intermarche said impacted stores had no choice but to "throw away all fresh and frozen products."
Leclerc told French news agency AFP that "a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," triggering "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores."

blocks.caption: Supermarkets say they had no choice but to throw away fresh and frozen food that was heated to over 50 degrees Celsius for several hours overnightImage: AFP

blocks.text: How were the refrigeration systems accessed?

The refrigeration systems targeted were reportedly from Danish supplier Danfoss, something suggested by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office, which reportedly identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor."
Danfoss said ​it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems," adding that the units in question "were running outdated firmware."
Danfoss said it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions."
Prime Minister Lecornu's office has tasked the French cybersecurity agency ANSSI with investigating the attack and is "liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected."

"Security issues" were also reported in Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, with Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize saying it had taken refrigeration systems offline to protect them, though the company added that it saw no connection to the French attacks.
Attacks on food supply now 'a reality'
It is currently unclear who could have been responsible for the cyberattack, and no group or individual has yet to claim responsibility.

The incident comes amid growing concern over vulnerabilities related to industrial ransomware and cyberattacks by malign actors in general, as well as heightened sensitivity toward Russian hybrid attacks in the midst of rising tensions over the war in Ukraine.

Last month, French President Emmanuel Macron — a strong supporter of Kyiv's self-defense against Russia — ordered measures put in place to protect France's critical infrastructure from Kremlin "hybrid attacks."

Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher, wrote on X: "Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable."

"Food security requires more attention at all levels," wrote EU Food and Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, who condemned the attack, adding that the "exploitation of food" is now a "reality."

articles.title: Poland reports arrests of 2 Turkish citizens in Germany in connection with Starlink station fire last month
articles.summary: Polish authorities have reported the arrests of two Turkish citizens in Germany in connection with alleged sabotage of a Starlink station last month. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the fire an act…

image.caption: Starlink has been a crucial tool for Ukraine's military since Russia's invasion in 2022Image: NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Polish officials on Monday said that two Turkish citizens have been detained in Germany in connection with a fire last month at a Starlink station in Poland.
The satellite-based Starlink internet service is widely used by the military of Poland's neighbor Ukraine amid the Russian invasion.
Officials from several EU countries have been warning of mounting Russian sabotage, cyber and hybrid attacks across Europe aiming either to erode support for Ukraine or to impact Ukraine directly.
Polish officials did not specify exactly where or when the two men were allegedly detained in Germany.
What did Poland say about the arrests and the case?
Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski reported the arrests on Monday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk following soon after.

"On behalf of Polish services, German police detained two Turkish citizens suspected of setting fire to a Starlink station in Masovia," he said on social media. "This is another act of hybrid warfare. The perpetrators of the sabotage will answer before the Polish justice system."
Masovia is the province that includes the Polish capital Warsaw, not that far from Poland's eastern borders to Belarus and Ukraine.
Poland blames Russia for incident
Poland's Special Services Minister Tomasz Siemoniak alleged that Russia was behind the incident.
He also told a press conference that, "​it is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning ​to individuals linked ‌to the criminal underworld" for such attacks.
Russia typically dismisses European claims of hybrid warfare or systemic sabotage as either anti-Russian hysteria or disinformation.
Will Elon Musk give Ukraine Starlink's eyes over Russia?

articles.title: Fact check: Viral videos falsely linked to Riyadh airport attacks
articles.summary: Many videos claiming to show an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport have gone viral online. DW Fact check analyzes some of the most-shared footage and finds evidence it was created…

image.caption: Riyadh's King Khalid International Aiport has been targeted by Yemen's Iran-backed HouthisImage: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in recent days. At least 16 people have been killed since last Thursday, according to Saudi authorities.

As news of the attacks spreads, social media users have been sharing videos that they claim show the strikes. While some authentic footage of the attacks and their aftermath has circulated online, DW Fact check found that several viral videos are not genuine and show signs of being AI-generated.

blocks.caption: This AI-generated video has been circulating since March and contains several inconsistenciesImage: X

blocks.text: Claim: This post with 1.7 million views on X, claims it shows the moment of an attack on the airport.
DW Fact check: Fake
The video has been online since March 2026 and could not show the most recent attacks on the airport.

Hectic camera movements and blurry footage help conceal glitches that often point to AI-generated content. However, our frame-by-frame analysis identified several inconsistencies. That suggests the video was AI-generated.

In the video, people run toward an exit as an explosion occurs outside. Despite the apparent danger, they continue moving toward the blast, seemingly through a glass door. This reaction is implausible.
Around 10 seconds into the video, an image of a hand holding a smartphone appears on the side of a man's head.
At 12 seconds, one man first appears not to have a hand, then miraculously has one.

blocks.caption: A side-by-side comparison shows a hand appear out of nowhereImage: X

blocks.text: Meta's AI identification tool finds AI signatures in the video and concludes it was created using generative AI.
Many shared the video as authentic, including the Times of Israel– its post had more than 256,000 views at the time of writing.
The video has appeared in many languages, including Arabic, English, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, Nepali, and it has been shared on YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Facebookand other platforms.
AI generates video from real photograph
Claim: In this post on X with 2.9 million views, a user claims it shows "new video footage of the moment King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh was targeted."

blocks.caption: AI can generate videos from still photographsImage: X

blocks.text: The video is AI-generated and contains several inconsistencies when compared with the real airport. Using a reverse image search, we found the photograph used to generate the fake video.

The original image was uploaded to stock photo database Shutterstockin 2016. Although it was taken from a slightly different angle it shows many visual cues that overlap with the video, including the white triangular geometric patterns of the airport building roof, the dome to the left, the luggage transport vehicles and the open and closed doors of the plane.

Other elements are missing. In the video, the light pole to the left of the aircraft appears without any lamps attached. The video is grainy and contains some visual glitches where parts of the image suddenly become blurry.

When the supposed missile strikes the plane, a nearby vehicle significantly changes its shape as it is thrown into the air. Another inconsistency is that, despite the missile's massive explosion and a resulting fireball, nearby objects do not cast corresponding shadows.
The account that shared the video has repeatedly posted AI-generated content in the past.
Whereas the October 8 attack at King Khalid International Airport did reportedly badly damage a plane, this video does not show the moment of attack.
Video predates attack and shows people move through objects
Claim: This TikTok postwith more than 301,000 views claims that the footage was recorded "just now from the heart of Riyadh Airport."

blocks.caption: AI-generated videos often contain impossible scenarios, like people walking through objectsImage: Tik Tok

blocks.text: This video had already circulated online in March 2026, months before the attack. We found the video was shared in Greek, Albanian, Turkish and Russian.

The footage contains several visual anomalies. Parts of the image appear blurry, and some people seem to merge into one another. In addition, a row of red lights in the terminal switches on one second before the supposed explosion becomes visible through the window.

The clearest indication that the video is AI-generated is the way people move through the queue barriers. At the beginning of the video, several people appear to walk directly through them. After the supposed explosion, some individuals run straight through barriers that appear to end mid-air and are connected on only one side.
Video contains Google AI watermarks
Claim: This TikTok post, which has garnered more than 500,000 views, reports on the attacks on the airports in Riyadh and Abha and includes a compilation of videos. We examined the first video.

blocks.caption: Since August 2026, the EU's AI Act requires AI-generated content to carry machine-readable markingsImage: Tik Tok

blocks.text: Analysis using Google Gemini detected that the video was generated, at least in part, with Google AI tools. The clip contains a SynthID watermark in both the images and the audio.

The same video also circulated on Facebook, where it has received more than 157,000 views. On Facebook it has been posted by an account that only shares AI-generated videos, and it is clearly labeled as "AI-content."

All four videos examined by DW Fact check are very short. Two are between six and ten seconds long, while the other two last 13 and 15 seconds, respectively. Such brief videos are easier to create with AI and often contain very little visual information, making it difficult for viewers to verify their authenticity.
Daniel Ebertz contributed to this research.
Fact check: How AI videos hijack your emotions in 8 seconds

articles.title: Germany: Labor Minister's resignation puts a spotlight on cracks within the government
articles.summary: Following the sudden resignation of Bärbel Bas as Labor Minister and co-chair of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), accusations are flying in Chancellor Merz's coalition government.

image.caption: Bärbel Bas' resignation sent shockwaves through Germany's governmentImage: Christophe Gateau/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The week kicked off with a bang: On Monday morning, Bärbel Bas announced her resignation as Labor Minister and as Co-Chair of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "Following the death of my stepdaughter, I realized that I need time to come to terms with my grief," Bärbel Bas wrote in a personal statement to party members.

However, she also cited "the public attacks against me — unfortunately, including some from within the ranks of our coalition partner" as reasons for her resignation. In fact, the pressure on Bas increased significantly in recent days. The centrist coalition government is urgently awaiting key legislative proposals from the Ministry of Labor.

Before the summer recess in July,a commission had already presented comprehensive proposals for reforming Germany's statutory pension system. The coalition partners of SPD and the center-right Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) wanted these proposals to be quickly turned into legislation. To date, however, no finalized drafts have been presented.
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
There had been calls for Bas' resignation

"The minister is no longer tenable. For months, she has been blocking the reforms our country so urgently needs," railed Christian von Stetten, head of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group's caucus representing medium-sized enterprises, said in reference to Bas in September.

In early October, such criticism was echoed by CDU Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, who demanded that the pension reform be passed by the end of the year. Bas had to submit the bill "promptly," Reiche said, although it was known at the time what a difficult personal situation her cabinet colleague was in at the time.

SPD co-leader, Finance Minister and Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil reacted sharply on Monday, saying the political attacks against Bas had been "disgraceful." Following a meeting of the SPD leadership, he told journalists in Berlin: "This poisons the political discourse, and — in the interest of preserving our political culture — I hope that everyone will take a step back and reflect on what has actually happened over the past few weeks." He called on all centrist politicians to be careful "that we don't destroy the good people in politics by attacking one another."
Such accusations carry significant weight at a time when the coalition is already mired in a deep crisis.

Adding to this is the new vacancy at the top of the SPD. Without Bas, Klingbeil will lead the SPD alone. A party convention will be scheduled for December or January to elect new leadership for the Social Democrats. It is not certain whether Klingbeil will run again. He had received a very poor result during his last reelection as party leader.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?
Swift replacement of Labor Minister

Alexander Schweitzer is to succeed Bärbel Bas as Federal Minister of Labor. The former state premier of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate had previously served as that state's Minister of Labor and Social Affairs. Chancellor Friedrich Merz expressed confidence that Schweitzer's experience would ensure " good cooperation within the federal government," adding that he hoped that the pending legislative proposals "will now be quickly approved by the cabinet and can be introduced into the parliamentary process."

The chancellor refuted the accusations leveled by Bas, saying that he had never discussed personal matters with her. Friedrich Merz said he had explicitly advised Bas to take the time she needed to grieve.
Merz promises change
Mistrust between the coalition partners has increased significantly, with SPD lawmakers speaking of an increasingly toxic political climate.

For months, the CDU and SPD have been grappling with low poll numbers, disappointing election results, and disputes over key reform projects. Plans for changes to the electricity tax, the introduction of a sugar tax, the pension and the labor market reform — hardly any initiative has been able to proceed without public controversy.

Adding to this is the crisis within the chancellor's party, the CDU, which saw a historic election defeat in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September, when it even lost representation in a state parliament for the first time in history.
On Sunday and Monday morning, therefore, the party leadership met for a closed-door session to discuss the way forward.

They produced a four-page document which indicates a shift in priorities, to put more emphasis on social issues: Affordable housing, lower electricity prices, better health care, and greater respect for citizens' lifetime achievements are mentioned in the paper. This is seen as a response to criticism that the CDU had been focusing too much on economic and regulatory issues.
Why Germany's political center is losing ground

The chancellor admitted that voters feel that politicians are not taking their hardships and fears of social decline seriously enough. "We have to work our way out of this slump — and get out of a crisis of confidence," Merz said. "You can't just reinvent a party overnight over a weekend, but we want to show that we're ready for change," the chancellor said, adding: "and we have to be, given the election results."
The chancellor announced that he would lower the electricity tax for everyone — a promise he had made before the general election in 2025 but had not kept.

With the closed-door meeting paper, the CDU is also sending a notable signal to the SPD. Instead of a programmatic shift further to the right, it is emphasizing its traditional social values — a stance that resonates well within the Social Democratic Party.

The chancellor made an effort to emphasize his intention to continue with the current coalition government: "The personnel changes will not call into question the basis of the coalition agreement," Merz said. He then repeated what he had recently said during a visit to Ukraine: "We need a stable federal government right now in order to remain capable of acting on the international stage."

Both CDU/CSU and SPD know that calling early elections could primarily benefit the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is leading in the polls nationwide. So despite the deep rifts, Lars Klingbeil and Friedrich Merz currently see no alternative to their coalition.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Despite the US president announcing energy infrastructure would not be targeted strikes have continued, Ukraine says.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on Monday
ByOlivia Ireland and Ella Kipling
Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".

There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.
He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."
"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.
Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.
On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.
Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.
Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".
On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.
Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, but it is not clear how many casualties there may be.
Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine?

When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".
For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.

Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.
In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.

Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.
However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."
Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman, BBC Verify

articles.title: Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire mean for Ukraine?
articles.summary: The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians face another winter with electricity outages.

blocks.text: US President Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that an energy ceasefire had been reached between Ukraine and Russia that was "effective immediately".
Ukraine's President Zelensky responded by saying his country is willing to back an energy ceasefire if Russia does the same, adding it could "become a major step toward ending the war".
However, Moscow hasn't confirmed its agreement and Zelensky said Russia hit a Ukrainian power plant in Kharkiv "immediately after" Trump's post on Sunday.
The BBC's Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians are facing another winter with electricity outages that leave people without heat, light or even water.

articles.title: US federal agents search home of Trump critic Ilhan Omar
articles.summary: Justice Department officials said the Washington residence of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, an outspoken opponent of President Trump, was raided as "part of an ongoing federal investigation."

image.caption: The US Justice Department did not share details of their investigationImage: Annabelle Gordon/REUTERS

blocks.text: US federal agents searched the home of a Democratic congresswoman and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump on Monday, the Department of Justice (DoJ) confirmed.
Officials from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US immigration enforcement, were seen early on Monday morning outside the Washington home of Ilhan Omar.

"Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice," a DoJ spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in a statement which didn't specifically name Omar.
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation."
Who is Ilhan Omar?

Omar, who came to the United States from Somalia as a child, was first elected to Congress in 2018 and is a member of the group of left-wing Democratic lawmakers known as "The Squad," who have been among Trump's most vocal opponents.
Omar represents a district including Minneapolis, home to one of the largest Somali communities in the US – a community which Trump has frequently targeted in racist outbursts.

blocks.caption: Omar has said Trump has a 'creepy obsession' with her Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: He ​previously called Somalis "garbage" and said in February that Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from."

Last ​week, Trump called Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan Abdul El Sayed a "RADICAL Extremist" and "Terrorist Sympathizer" while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers
Democrats decry 'abuse of power'
House Democratic leaders condemned the search as an "abuse of power" by the Trump administration.
Omar said she will “not be silenced” and called the search of her home the “latest escalation” in President Donald Trump’s '‘intimidation" campaign.

blocks.caption: Trump has been accused of weaponizing US agenices to go after his political opponentsImage: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Omar has called Trump's focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession" said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes ⁠to "hateful political rhetoric" especially ​from Trump.
On Monday, Omar said she will "not be silenced" and called the search of her home the "latest escalation" in Trump's "intimidation" campaign.

No charges against Omar were announced in connection with Monday's search, but US media reported that the operation was linked to a criminal fraud investigation into immigration paperwork submitted on her behalf by her late father when she was a child.
The search comes just three weeks before midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans will be trying to defend their thin majorities in the US.

articles.title: Why the US is bringing back firing squads
articles.summary: Medical experts and those who study the death penalty say each method can go wrong and cause severe pain.

blocks.text: Warning: this story contains upsetting descriptions of executions
America's use of the death penalty is under the spotlight once again after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the military would livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan.
The former military psychiatrist fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009.
His execution would be the first time the US Army had used a firing squad since 1945, a method that several states already authorise to put people to death.
And it comes on the heels of the botched death by lethal injection of Christa Pike - a woman convicted of murdering her classmate.
Pike was taken to hospital and then discharged to prison 10 days later, after making a recovery from the failed attempt, her lawyers said.

Amid rising concerns over botched executions - and renewed federal support for the death penalty - the US has introduced both new and old forms of execution like firing squads, the electric chair and the gas chamber.
Lethal injection, which was first used in Texas in 1982, is now the most common way people are executed across the US, with many states making it their default method.

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery based in Atlanta, Georgia, said states turned to lethal injection because it appeared from the outside to be a more peaceful means of execution.
"That was a myth," he said.
Dr Zivot said that sometimes the injection of the drugs can cause pulmonary edema, when a person's lungs fill with fluid, which can give people the painful sensation of drowning.
"It's a terrifying way to die - to drown," he said.

Other times, people have medical conditions, like Pike - who suffered from thrombocytosis and other medical problems her lawyers warned about - that can complicate the execution and make it more painful.
During Pike's failed execution, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.
There are a host of reasons why so many lethal injections have been botched, but some of the same factors persist, said Maher.

"Oftentimes, the executions go wrong because training of staff is inadequate, because drugs are degraded or expired or improperly stored, or because states are experimenting with different combinations of drugs that have never been used before," she said.
In light of many of these challenges, some states have turned to executing people with a new and controversial method: nitrogen gas.
Alabama and Louisiana are the first states to have carried out executions with nitrogen gas, though three other states - Arkansas, Mississippi and Oklahoma - also allow for it.
Two years ago, Alabama used nitrogen gas to execute Kenneth Eugene Smith, after a botched attempt to put him to death via lethal injection in 2022.
During the execution, which took 25 minutes, Smith thrashed violently on the gurney as he was given the gas, a witness told the BBC at the time.
The method involves forcing a prisoner to breathe pure nitrogen gas until they suffocate.
Dr Zivot said people who breathe in the gas sometimes get seizures. Alabama has executed seven people using nitrogen gas since introducing the method in January 2024.
"Each time it was a horror show of struggling, of moving, of seizing," Dr Zivot said.
While some states have explored new methods, others have reauthorised some of the earliest ways US officials used to put people to death.
As of this year, nine states have approved execution by electric chair, with South Carolina using it as their default method.
Electrocution "has a horrible history of botched executions", Maher said, and errors with these executions is one of the reasons why states introduced lethal injections in the first place.
In 1997, Pedro Medina's head caught fire as he was put to death in an electric chair in Florida.
"A solid flame covered his whole head, from one side to the other. I had the impression of somebody being burned alive," his attorney Mike Minerva said, according to the Los Angeles Times.
A method once used as punishment in the military and in times of war, firing squad executions have also proven susceptible to human error.

Mikahl Mahdi was executed by a three-person firing squad last year after admitting to killing an off-duty police officer in 2004. But his lawyers say his death was prolonged because the bullets missed his heart and instead hit his liver and other organs.

In July, Idaho became the first state to use a firing squad as its primary method of execution after it ran into issues with lethal injections. Mississippi, Oklahoma, Utah and South Carolina also authorise this execution method.

Alonzo Lunsford, a former US Army sergeant who survived being shot seven times by Hasan in the Fort Hood attack, told the BBC the firing squad was a "befitting" method to end his life because lethal injection and a gas chamber would be "doing him a favour".

Hanging was the main method of execution in the US until the 1890s, and several Asian countries including Japan and Singapore still use this method. But in the US, no states authorise hanging because of its "terrible" history, Maher said.
"Hanging has such a terrible association with racial violence and lynching in the states," she said. "So that is why there's no state that's using hanging or has authorised that method to be used."
Trump - a proponent of the death penalty - brought back the federal death penalty when he returned to office in 2025, after Joe Biden's administration put a moratorium on federal executions in 2021.

"Capital punishment is an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens," his office wrote in an executive order.
Maher said there has been "quite a bit of activity" in state legislatures to approve and reauthorise other methods of execution since Trump began expressing enthusiasm for the death penalty.

Trump has called for the death penalty to be expanded to punish large-scale drug dealers, human traffickers and those who kill police officers. Over the past 50 years, all prisoners who received death sentences were convicted of murder, though capital punishment was also used for rape convictions before that.

Asked by reporters whether Pike's failed lethal injection should spur changes to the death penalty, Trump did not directly answer the question, adding that the execution method "shouldn't be very difficult".

articles.title: Starlink India launch: Why Elon Musk is still waiting
articles.summary: Despite securing key approvals, the Starlink satellite internet service remains in regulatory limbo, raising questions about security clearances, competition and India’s investment climate.

image.caption: Musk last week blamed unnamed Indian 'oligarchs' for delaying Starlink's launchImage: rokas91/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, has escalated his criticism of the delay in launching Starlink in India. Last week, he sarcastically referred to Mukesh Ambani, one of India's richest people and chairman of Reliance Industries, as "Prime Minister Ambani" and accused his supporters of protecting a monopoly.
"Would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?" Musk wrote on X, arguing that the service could bring internet access to underserved communities across India.

Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, joined the discussion, writing: "Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy." Musk replied: "Thank you, Rahul. This is indeed troubling."
A delayed launch and a war of words
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) accused Gandhi of championing Musk's interests, while party leaders defended the government's handling of the issue.

Speaking during the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi last week, Reliance Jio chairman Akash Ambani declined to comment on Musk's remarks. He said: "I have no comments to make. We want to keep our heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Akash, Mukesh Ambani's eldest son, also noted that Jio was progressing on its own end-to-end indigenous satellite broadband technology stack.
Meanwhile, Starlink — despite securing key approvals and signing distribution agreements with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel — has yet to begin commercial operations in India.
Its low-earth-orbit satellites could provide internet access in remote villages, hilly regions and border areas where fiber-optic networks and mobile towers are expensive to build.
But the service would enter a market where mobile data is inexpensive and established telecom operators have extensive networks.

blocks.caption: Musk said he would price Starlink's satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Ambani's low-cost Reliance Jio [FILE: February 13, 2025]Image: Pib/Press Information/Planet Pix/ZUMA Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: India's Ministry of Communications says security assessments for all three licensed satellite operators are under way and that they are at broadly the same regulatory stage.

In a statement, the ministry said every licensee must meet security conditions intended to protect users and their data. Once an assessment is completed, an operator can seek spectrum assignment. It described allegations that the framework was unfair or discriminatory as "baseless and misconceived."
Legitimate security concerns?

Starlink secured a satellite communications licence from the Department of Telecommunications and authorization from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center in 2025. These approvals do not automatically permit commercial operations, however.

The security debate surrounding Starlink has intensified following remarks by BJP leader Nishikant Dubey, who chairs a parliamentary committee. In a post on X on October 11, Dubey said the panel had examined Starlink's security challenges.
"As the chairman of the parliamentary committee, our committee has understood the challenges facing the country's security agencies through Starlink," he wrote in Hindi language.
Responding to Musk's criticism, Dubey added: "India is a healthy democratic, sovereign nation, and it does not change its security policy under pressure from social media or external figures."
Dubey did not specify the security risks or regulatory requirements holding up the launch.

blocks.caption: ​India is one of the world's biggest ‌internet markets [FILE: August 21, 2022]Image: Ashish Vaishnav/Zuma/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former intelligence officer and national security expert Yashovardhan Jha Azad said the impasse reflected commercial competition, regulatory uncertainty and legitimate security concerns.
"The central question is: who retains effective control over an essential communications service during a crisis?" Azad told DW.
He said India needed safeguards covering traffic routing, lawful interception under due process and cybersecurity.

"The existence of security requirements, however, does not establish why Starlink's application remains pending," Azad said. He pointed out that the government has not publicly detailed which specific conditions, if any, the company still needs to satisfy.
Investment, manufacturing and affordability
The delay in Starlink's launch has raised questions about the predictability of India's investment environment.

Economist Lekha Chakrabarty, who has studied the issue closely, said the problem was not that India was shutting its doors to foreign investment, but that companies could not plan around an open-ended approval process.
"The Starlink impasse is best read not as India closing its door to foreign investment, but as a failure to make an already open door predictably passable," Chakrabarty told DW.
She said security reviews were necessary given the sensitivity of satellite communications, which involve critical infrastructure, cross-border data, gateway control and lawful interception.
But the problem, she said, was the lack of transparency around approval criteria and timelines.
"Investors can price known rules, they cannot efficiently price discretionary, multi-agency processes with uncertain endpoints," Chakrabarty added.
World seeks wider web as US dominates satellite internet

Pankaj Mohindroo, chairman of the India Cellular and Electronics Association, said Starlink's entry could create opportunities for Indian electronics manufacturers in satellite terminals, antennas, communication modules and network equipment.

"India already has a strong trusted electronics manufacturing base, which provides an opportunity for global technology companies to develop local partnerships and strengthen domestic supply chains," he told DW.

articles.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
articles.summary: Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

blocks.text: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Hackers reportedly gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight.
The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.
More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while at least 300 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, according to the AFP news agency.
Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.
Some supermarket staff reportedly said they were hit by waves of hot air when they opened freezer units on Monday morning.
French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.
Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.

The Paris prosecutor's office told AFP it had opened an investigation into the incident, which it called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

Eoropean Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."
The full scale of the attack is so far unclear.

Reports in specialist retail and local media said stores from other food giants, including Carrefour, E.Leclerc and Monoprix, were also attacked. BBC News has approached the supermarket chains for comment.
In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".
He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

articles.title: Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?
articles.summary: The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV had only recently returned from a trip to France when he announced doctors had found a nodule on his lungImage: Grzegorz Galazka/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.
At under 3 cm (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.
In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.
What we know so far
All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."
That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.
Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.
